#3597. 8 Near-Perfect Fantasy Miniseries That Hook You in the First Episode

Eight magical worlds with shorter stories still worth getting lost in

Fantasy television has given us some of the most imaginative stories ever told, transporting viewers to magical kingdoms, mysterious alternate realities, and worlds filled with creatures that shouldn't exist. Shows like Game of Thrones and Rings of Power dominate the conversation, pushing some of the genre's best storytelling to the forefront, but there’s something to be said of the smaller productions and shorter stories.

Miniseries offer a unique opportunity to explore extraordinary settings and compelling characters without stretching their stories across multiple, seemingly endless seasons. From beloved literary adaptations to wonderfully strange animated adventures, these eight fantasy miniseries prove that you don't need hundreds of episodes to build an unforgettable world.

While its name might sound a little too ridiculous for most, Terry Pratchett's Hogfather offers a rather eccentric introduction to the mythology of Discworld, arguably one of fantasy literature's most imaginative settings. The two-part miniseries focuses on Susan Sto Helit (Michelle Dockery), the granddaughter of Death himself in her investigation into the disappearance of the Hogfather — the Discworld equivalent of Santa Claus.

While Susan hunts for answers, Death (Ian Richardson) reluctantly takes over the sleigh to keep the holiday spirit intact, even as a sinister conspiracy works to erase humanity's capacity for belief. Hogfather balances clashes between guild assassins and oblivious wizards with Pratchett's trademark wit hiding a moving story about imagination and the quiet necessity of magic underneath all the festive absurdity.

Fairy tales have inspired countless fantasy adventures, but few television productions have had as much fun upending classic folklore as the 2000 miniseries The 10th Kingdom. The story kicks off when reluctant New Yorker Tony Lewis (John Larroquette) and his daughter Virginia (Kimberly Williams) fall through a magical portal into the Nine Kingdoms, a sprawling parallel world governed by the descendants of Snow White, Cinderella, and Little Red Riding Hood. As one might expect, they quickly discover that life following "happily ever after" is messy, corrupt, and deeply dangerous.

Caught in the crossfire of the Evil Queen's (Dianne Wiest) ruthless plot to seize power, Tony and Virginia go on the run with a golden retriever who happens to be the rightful Prince Wendell (Daniel Lapaine) and Wolf (Scott Cohen), a hopelessly smitten half-wolf fighting his own carnivorous urges. Driven by an oversized cast of colorful oddballs and a self-aware sense of humor, The 10th Kingdom transforms familiar fairy tale tropes into a delightfully unpredictable adventure for the small screen.

Blending police procedural grit with surreal science fiction, BBC Two’s critically acclaimed two-part adaptation of China Miéville’s The City & The City is hard not to recommend. Inspector Tyador Borlú (David Morrissey) investigates the brutal murder of a foreign student found dumped in a grimy European city called Besźel, a place that occupies the exact same physical space as Ul Qoma, its ultra-modern twin metropolis. The two distinct populations are strictly conditioned to "unsee" one another and their overlapping architecture, effectively living in separate parallel realities despite sharing the same streets.

As Borlú’s investigation crosses dangerous and forbidden borders, he soon uncovers a conspiracy that challenges everything he understands about his world. Anchored by Morrissey's methodical performance, the miniseries delivers an intellectually fascinating mystery you’ll have to see to believe.

Sure, it might lean more into the sci-fi and superhero categories, but HBO's Watchmen is still a surprisingly worthwhile hit for fantasy buffs. Set in an alternate version of America decades after the events of Alan Moore and Dave Gibbons' groundbreaking graphic novel of the same name, the nine-episode miniseries follows Angela Abar (Regina King), a Tulsa police detective who operates under the masked identity Sister Night.

As she investigates a conspiracy involving white supremacists, the police, and some very powerful individuals, the series gradually reveals a much stranger story involving godlike beings, extraordinary abilities, and the nature of time itself. King is phenomenal, and Damon Lindelof delivers one of television's most ambitious superhero stories, one filled with grit and emotion. Despite its fan backlash, Watchmen is a terrific show that deserves to be experienced in its full entirety.

Originally conceived as a 1996 BBC Two six-part miniseries before Neil Gaiman adapted it into a bestselling novel, Neverwhere takes an ordinary London commuter and drops him into one of the most imaginative urban fantasy settings ever designed for television. The story follows Richard Mayhew (Gary Bakewell), a mild-mannered Scottish securities analyst whose impulsive decision to help an injured young woman named Door (Laura Fraser) causes him to slip through the cracks and effectively disappear from the world above.

Unable to return to his former life, Richard finds himself navigating London Below, a bizarre underground society populated by a slew of eccentric inhabitants who exist beyond the awareness of ordinary people. His journey alongside Door becomes an increasingly dangerous adventure filled with strange encounters and unexpected revelations. Although its modest production values show their age, Neverwhere remains an imaginative piece of fantasy television for any fan of the genre.

Gormenghast isn’t like normal fantasy tales, dropping the familiar dragons and magic in favor of a decaying Gothic castle where centuries-old rituals dictate all aspects of everyday life. Based on Mervyn Peake's celebrated novels, this four-part miniseries begins with the birth of Titus Groan, heir to the ancient castle's ruling family. His arrival coincides with the escape of Steerpike, an ambitious kitchen servant determined to climb the castle's social hierarchy by manipulating its eccentric inhabitants.

Across four decadent episodes, Peake's enormous gothic castle becomes the stage for a wonderfully bizarre tale of ruthless ambition and festering political intrigue. Driven by its suffocating atmosphere, eccentric cast of characters, and surreal visual design, Gormenghast feels unlike almost anything else in the fantasy genre.

Although an animated miniseries, Patrick McHale's 2014 Cartoon Network production Over the Garden Wall feels like a long-forgotten American folktale brought to life. Across ten 11-minute chapters, anxious teenager Wirt (Elijah Wood) and his optimistic younger half-brother Greg (Collin Dean) wander lost through the Unknown, an autumnal forest populated by colonial-era townsfolk, anthropomorphic frogs, and sinister supernatural figures. Guided by a cynical bluebird named Beatrice (Melanie Lynskey), the siblings search for a path home while evading the Beast (Samuel Ramey), a shadowy entity that stalks lost travelers and feeds on their despair.

McHale and his team pair hand-painted backgrounds inspired by vintage storybook illustrations with a Grammy-nominated soundtrack steeped in early-20th-century Americana. Beneath that nostalgic surface sits a surprisingly dark and emotionally resonant allegory about guilt and the terror of growing up, cementing Over the Garden Wall as one of the finest fantasy miniseries ever produced.

A smoke break at the Signature Theatre ultimately resulted in one of Lois Smith‘s most fascinating performances. The Tony Award winner met Zane Pais while they were both grabbing a quick cigarette while rehearsing plays. Pais had been an admirer of Smith’s work in stage productions like “The Inheritance” and films such as “Marjorie Prime” and “Five Easy Pieces,” and longed to collaborate.

“She has the most amazing delivery of lines; she’s always able to do something so unexpected with the language,” Pais said during a recent Zoom interview with Smith. “I’ve seen Lois my whole life in so many amazing shows, just be so unbelievably present on stage and be such a generous actor, and just give these heartfelt and unexpected performances. I’m a big fucking fan.” Related Stories Is A24 Finally Big Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio? Bill Hader’s Feature Directorial Debut ‘They Know’ Lands at Black Bear

So Pais wrote a short film, “Lightning Bug,” with Smith in mind. In it, she plays Lydia, a fiercely independent nonagenarian who is being pressured into selling the family home by her son and granddaughter. But things take an unexpected turn when a strange young man crashes their dinner, giving Lydia a chance to demonstrate she hasn’t missed a step despite her advanced age.

“It was all there in the script,” Smith, who recently turned 96, said. “It wasn’t complex for me to pull it off even though the script is complex.”

The role did require Smith to perform some fight choreography, but she seemed more nervous about singing a song on screen.

“I really worried: Am I going to be able to do this?” Smith said. “They made me a tape, and I listened to it and listened to it and practiced. I was nervous, but it went all right.”

“Lightning Bug” filmed over a weekend in the upstate New York home of one of Pais’s relatives. It was true no-frills, all-hands effort. The cast and crew bunked in an Airbnb, and a friend of Pais’s cooked meals for everyone.

“It felt like we were part of a theater troupe,” Pais said. “We’d work hard. Then in the evenings, we would have red wine and smoke cigarettes.”

“I seldom smoke,” Smith interjected. “Occasionally, I’ll smoke other people’s cigarettes.”

#3594. Apple TV's 10/10 Spy Thriller Just Made a Totally Ambitious Move

Julio is a Senior Author for Collider. He studied History and International Relations at university, but found his calling in cultural journalism. When he isn't writing, Julio also teaches English at a nearby school. He has lived in São Paulo most of his life, where he covers CCXP and other big events. Having loved movies, music, and TV from an early age, he prides himself in knowing every minute detail about the things he loves. When he is older, he dreams of owning a movie theater in a small countryside town.

The best news for fans of spy thrillers this week isn't what you'd expect. While everyone was celebrating a new James Bond, MI5 actually had the biggest shake-up as Apple TV announced the renewal of Slow Horses for Seasons 9 and 10. You read that right — Season 6 has barely wrapped up, and viewers can already look forward to four more seasons of Jackson Lamb's (Gary Oldman) trademark grumpiness. This comes as a great surprise, not just the number of seasons itself, but given the greater circumstances. Back in September, Apple had already renewed Slow Horses for Season 8, and now, less than two months later, has confirmed an incredible Season 10 update. It's a really unprecedented move for any streamer, so is there a catch — or are things just that good at Slough House?

Gone are the golden years of cable TV, when viewers could expect their favorite shows to return year after year without fail. Getting lost in series like Friends, Supernatural, and Grey's Anatomy was a pleasure, but, with the dawn of the streaming age, it became harder and harder to find such long-running shows — so much so that people usually point to these behemoths of old when looking for long-term commitment on TV, as those titles remain available on most streaming platforms.

Because of the usual budget constraints, long-term casting commitments, and ever-changing business models, scripted live-action shows rarely go beyond six or seven seasons on streaming, so Slow Horses earning this type of renewal is completely unprecedented in the current landscape. Its now-confirmed 10-season run makes it Apple TV's longest-running series — a title it previously shared with For All Mankind, which is slated to end with Season 6.

There are a few reasons that have resulted in Slow Horses getting this kind of treatment. Each season has only six episodes, making it much quicker to produce, and every season finale delivers a preview for the next batch of episodes. Most important, though, is how well it performs among audiences and critics. On Rotten Tomatoes, every season of Slow Horses has consistently performed above 95%, so, from a business perspective, what's not to love about it?

On its own, this unexpected renewal is bound to keep Slow Horses and Apple TV at the top of viewers' minds for a while, especially with a new season set to premiere next year. Its consistent release schedule is another reason this series has performed so well since the beginning. (Longer gaps between seasons are another streaming staple, unfortunately.) To keep the pace, a quick production is important, but what's really vital is the fact that there has always been source material available to adapt for each new season.

Slow Horses famously adapts Mick Herron's Slough House book series, which currently comprises nine entries. From the beginning, each season has adapted one book, with the exception being Season 6 — which adapted two novels, Joe Country and Slough House. Right now, the expectation is that Season 7 will adapt Bad Actors and Season 8 will adapt Clown Town, Herron's most recent novel published in 2025.

The line between reality and fiction might be clear, but these misfit spies' pulse-pounding missions are definitely rooted in truth.

Now that Slow Horses has been renewed for more, though, Seasons 9 and 10 don't yet have a published Herron novel to adapt — at least for now. The expectation is that a tenth Slough House novel will be announced, although there has been no confirmation as of this writing. Herron has previously mentioned that he already knows "why, when, and where Jackson Lamb dies," so it stands to reason that the Apple TV series won't run forever, and its end may be steadily approaching.

Even if Herron's tenth novel takes longer to reach publication than anticipated, there are still five Slough House novellas for the show to draw from, all compiled in Watch the Quiet Snow. It's still way too early to know where Slow Horses is headed in Seasons 9 and 10, but it seems unlikely that Apple TV would take such a bold step in renewing it without a clear plan.

Curiously, the timing of this renewal news couldn't have been better. Mere days prior, Olivia Cooke, who plays Sidonie "Sid" Baker, said in an interview that Season 8 would be Slow Horses' last, even mentioning that the cast has been "all melancholy" while filming. Apple TV's renewal immediately refutes this, adding another two seasons to the previously announced seventh and eighth back in September. (Hopefully, Season 8 isn't Cooke's last season, though.)

Finally, there is the "James Bond" of it all. Jack Lowden, who plays down-on-his-luck protagonist River Cartwright, was among the top contenders for 007, but although fans rooted for him until the very end, the role ultimately went to Robert Pattinson. Ironically, hoping to get out of Slough House for a better position in a government agency only to ultimately get shot down is such a Cartwright thing that we can almost hear Lamb laughing in the background. So far, only Oldman's return has been confirmed, but it's hard to imagine Slow Horses without the rest of Lamb's joes, no matter how many seasons the show ultimately runs for.

#3592. Everything We Know About GTA 7

Because it's never too early to spam YouTube comments

Grand Theft Auto 6 has only just been released, so it might seem a bit early to start thinking about Grand Theft Auto 7. I swear I’m not just writing an “Everything we know about GTA 7” article just so I can stuff a post with the “Everything we know about GTA 7” keyword and have Polygon own “Everything we know about GTA 7” search queries. That would be quite a gambit.

Especially for a search term as competitive as “Everything we know about GTA 7.”

But the truth is there actually are some infinitesimal snippets of information already making the rounds about GTA 7. It can feel like grasping at straws; again, GTA 6 only just came out. But it’s never too early to start the “GTA 7 when???” conversation in the comments section of every Game Awards and State of Play YouTube stream. Here’s everyth– oh, you know the drill.

The wait for GTA 6 has been atypically long — for the series, for its developer, and for video games on the whole. It’s been 13 years since GTA 5, eight years since Red Dead Redemption 2. Until now, Rockstar Games hadn’t even released a game for this console generation, which, if timelines for the PlayStation 6 and Xbox’s Project Helix are to be believed, will start winding down in a year or two.

In an interview ahead of GTA 6’s release, Rockstar North co-studio head Rob Nelson told Polygon that the studio’s map team started work as early as 2015. 2015! Remember how young we were? Remember how innocent we were? Remember how many fewer grays I had? Not that one? OK.

One of the reasons GTA 6’s development took so long was because, alongside making the game, Rockstar has also been refining the technology and processes needed to make games of this scale in the first place.

“The engine, the tools, and the team we’ve built during this project will allow us to do things more quickly,” GTA 6 co-head of development Phil Hooker told Bloomberg. “I feel confident that we can build on top of this and go more sideways than upwards to build more compelling content.”

“We foundationally changed a lot of stuff on this project,” added Rockstar North co-head Aaron Garbut during that same interview. “But now it’s done, and we’re not going to rip it apart.”

There’s also the fact that Rockstar employs close to 5,000 people today, more than double it did around the end of development for Red Dead Redemption 2 in 2018.

In a sprawling Guardian profile ahead of GTA 6’s release, Nelson suggested the series might eventually move beyond its signature satirical version of the United States, but that the studio still had its eye on America for the time being.

“Never say never, but there’s still so much to do in America,” Nelson said. “It doesn’t matter where you live … no one experiences the America that we’re portraying here in its fullness.”

Previous Grand Theft Auto games have been set in major metropolitan areas like Los Angeles (Los Santos) and New York City (Liberty City). But even if Rockstar opts not to return to a previously seen location, there are plenty of cultural American hubs to satirize, including Chicago, Seattle, Boston, Washington, D.C., and New Orleans (a 19-century version of which appeared in Red Dead Redemption 2 as Saint Denis).

Let’s imagine Rockstar does leap straight from GTA 6 to a hypothetical GTA 7, as opposed to pivoting to long-desired sequels to either Red Dead Redemption 2 or Bully. We won’t hear about whatever the studio’s next game is for a long time, according to Strauss Zelnick, CEO of Rockstar parent company Take-Two Interactive. He all but said as much in an interview with TBPN (on Nov. 19, GTA 6’s release date, no less).

“We at Take-Two just went live with GTA 6 on Nov. 19. Wait, let me check my watch… Oh, it’s still Nov. 19,” Zelnick said. “I mean, guys, really? My father-in-law had a line about how whenever he had many great business achievements and a lot of admirers, and if he ever said anything nice, he’d say, ‘Oh, those are yesterday’s headlines.’ But it’s not even yesterday!”

Before Rockstar even revealed a release date for GTA 6, fans of the series began riffing on GTA 7 in a dedicated subreddit. Yes, it’s intentionally tongue-in-cheek, with winking suggestions for its setting (Harrisburg, PA) and features (“will there be car?”), but it gets at the heart why such a thing can resonate in the modern internet in the first place: GTA 6 took a reallllllllllly long time. And as any Elder Millennial (or their therapists) will tell you, humor is a pretty effective coping mechanism.

In fact, even GTA 6 has gotten in on the GTA 7 memes. Early in the game, as pointed out by some GTA fans on Reddit, you can see an in-game social media post quipping about the excruciating wait for a game called Race and Chase 7. The original name for Grand Theft Auto’s pitch, back in the ‘90s? Race ‘n’ Chase.

#3591. Sunrise On The Reaping's 10 Biggest Changes To The Hunger Games Book

Warning! This post contains SPOILERS for The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

The newest addition to the Hunger Games franchise, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, has officially hit theaters, and while the movie's Rotten Tomatoes scores currently reflect the fact that it's a hit, at least in terms of the history of this franchise, fans will no doubt be pretty surprised to realize how much of the book was altered or cut. Reviews of Sunrise on the Reaping have highlighted the film's dedication to the original story, and for the most part, that's fair. The movie is loyal to Suzanne Collins work in myriad ways.

However, that doesn't mean that all the major plot points, scenes, and highly anticipated moments were included. On the contrary, there is a frankly shocking number of alterations to the source material, some of them quite significant, and they really do change the story at various points. From changes to the Katniss and Peeta cameo to a complete overhaul of the book's approach to the violence, here are the 10 biggest changes the Sunrise on the Reaping movie makes.

Although Haymitch suffers many brutalities and losses in Sunrise on the Reaping, easily one of the biggest is the loss of his girlfriend, Lenore Dove. In both the book and the movie, Lenore Dove dies because Snow is seeking to punish Haymitch, and he does so, in part, by having Haymitch unknowingly feed Lenore Dove poison gumdrops. Even worse, Haymitch realizes what is happening before Lenore Dove dies, but he can't do anything to save her; he just sits helplessly as she dies in his arms.

For the most part, those story beats remain the same in Sunrise on the Reaping. However, in the book, Haymitch's grieving looks different. Specifically, in the book, Haymitch ends up spending an entire day sleeping on her grave. The book specifies that he does this from sun up to sun down to sun up again. In the movie, his grief is still incredibly evident, but audiences don't see him unable to move from atop her grave as he does in the book, and that no doubt would have packed an even greater emotional punch.

Along with the way Haymitch grieves being slightly different in the movie, the conversation that President Snow and Haymitch have about Lenore Dove before the Hunger Games begin is altered in the movie. In the book, Snow is only aware that Lenore Dove is Covey after watching the Reaping, and he unsettles Haymitch by asking what her color name is, making it clear that he knows of the Covey (which, Hunger Games fans will immediately understand, is because of his own prior romance with Lucy Gray).

In the movie, however, Snow reveals that he already knows exactly who Lenore Dove is. While it might seem like a small alteration, this does significantly reframe the nature of their conversation. And, in fact, those differences are only all the greater because, in the book, it is President Snow, in this scene, who reveals that Lenore Dove wrote an inscription on the back of the flint striker she had gifted him for his birthday. In the movie, Haymitch already knows.

Yet another change that specifically connects to the Covey, in the book, Haymitch actually gets to see Lucy Gray's Hunger Games, becoming the only person anywhere around his age who has done so. He is actually forced to watch them after he makes it out of the arena, in a sequence that is entirely removed from the movie (for example, after surviving the arena, Haymitch is also forced to attend a party and then is stuck inside of a golden cage while people from the Capitol feed him).

Audiences were hoping to see a shot of Lucy Gray because of this, but she never appears in the movie. This is, honestly, a surprising choice for the movie, as it would no doubt have been very easy to incorporate that footage from The Hunger Games: The Ballad of Sonbirds and Snakes. It actually seemed like a no-brainer to incorporate this, so the decision not to remains a mystery. Perhaps, it was simply a matter of cutting down the time.

Lucy Gray wasn't the only former District 12 victor that appeared in the book; all four actually played a role in the movie. For Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark, in both the book and the movie, that included an appearance in the epilogue, which is set after the original Hunger Games trilogy. The movie largely keeps what was included in the book, with the trio sharing the screen again as proof that they have, finally, truly survived the Hunger Games and the Capitol.

However, fans of the novel will note that there were some changes here. Among the most significant was the removal of Katniss bringing goose eggs to Haymitch so that he could raise them. The novel confirms that this is because Haymitch has shared that his lost love, Lenore Dove, cared for geese. Because of that emotional significance, many fans were expecting to see this moment; however, the film opted not to include it.

Perhaps almost as anticipated as the scene in which Katniss presents Haymitch with goose eggs was the scene from the book in which Haymitch overhears Silka—the career, who is ultimately the one he ends up going head-to-head with in the final fight—crying and drops some chocolate for her. For those who haven't read the book, that might seem like it isn't the biggest deal, but this was actually an incredibly important moment in the book.

Specifically, this moment was meant to remind audiences that even the careers are still just scared kids in the Hunger Games, who are doing what they think they have to do to survive. It's easy to forget that, whether it's on the page or on the screen, because the careers in particular are depicted as so ruthless. That was exactly why this scene mattered, though, and it's a shame that it was cut. As a result, Silka doesn't read as a sympathetic character, at least not nearly to the same degree, and that's a disappointing change.

Yet another major book moment that Sunrise on the Reaping fans will be shocked to see excluded from the movie is the scene in which Maritte (a District 4 career tribute who is barely in the movie) and Maysilee Donner kill three Gamemakers who have entered the arena during the Hunger Games. This is a massive event in the book, for several reasons. For one, this is a monumental and jarring thing for the tributes to do, as its such open rebellion against the Capitol—not shocking in the case of Maysilee, but much more shocking in the case of Maritte.

For another, in the book, this becomes a serious moment of tension between Haymitch and Maysilee, as Haymitch fails to act, and Maysilee, understandably, is furious, pointing out that it should be Haymitch fighting to protect her, not Maritte. Additionally, though, in the book, this action is effectively why Maysilee is marked for death in the Games. In the movie, that's positioned largely as something that's done just to punish Haymitch. That's also a shame, as it takes away some of Maysilee's agency.

Among the more disturbing plot points of Sunrise on the Reaping is that, after District 12's Louella, also called Haymitch's sweetheart throughout the book, dies in the chariot accident before the Games, she is replaced by a body double who insists she is Louella. Of course, she isn't, and that's just the Capitol being more evil than ever, but the tributes have to pretend it is. Ultimately, they call her Lou Lou and accept her as their own.

While that basic arc is kept, many of the major details about Lou Lou aren't. For one, the book reveals that Lou Lou is from District 11 because she recognizes songs from that district. More significantly, in the book, Lou Lou has an ear piece through which the Capitol can listen to and control her and a drug pump attached to her chest for them to subdue her. In the movie, she has neither, which already takes some of the bite out of how horrific the Capitol is. This also means Haymitch doesn't mercy kill her by pulling her pump out in the movie, as he does in the book.

Shockingly, the Sunrise on the Reaping movie also doesn't show the scores of the tributes, despite that being a massive part of the original Hunger Games trilogy and a significant part of the book, nor does it really emphasize sponsors or gifts during the Hunger Games at all. In terms of the former, that is genuinely surprising because Haymitch receiving a 1 as his score is a major plot detail in the book (and proves that the Capitol had it out for him right from the jump, which everyone in Panem knew as soon as that 1 popped up).

Additionally, sponsors and gifts are a huge part of the Hunger Games, and in the Sunrise on the Reaping book in particular, they are prominent in part because Haymitch is consistently sent gifts in the arena (including the chocolate that, in the book, he drops to Silka). This leads to multiple very sweet moments between Haymitch and Maysilee in which they share a picnic, with Haymitch even giving Maysilee the elegant glass he received in one gift.

Coinciding with the absence of the gifts in the arena was the absence of many key moments between Haymitch and Maysilee in the books. Yes, in the movie it's still clear that they become like siblings and have a genuine love for one another, but in the book, they actually say this directly, with Maysilee at one point telling Haymitch that she will be his sister. They also go through myriad other situations together, only some of which is captured in the movie.

Their time together in the arena is actually cut so short that audiences don't even see things like one keeping watch while the other sleeps, because there simply isn't enough time passing on screen for that. This is yet another huge surprise, not only because it's one of fans' most beloved aspects of the book but also because Mckenna Grace and Joseph Zada are incredibly talented actors with plenty of fan backing and great chemistry on screen; it would have been brilliant to see more of these scenes with them.

Finally, the single biggest difference between Sunrise on the Reaping as a book and a movie is the level of blood and gore—and that extends throughout the entire movie. For example, when the squirrels attack Ampert in the book, it is said that only a skeleton remained; there was no flesh or muscle left on him. In the movie, however, he really only has (visually, at least) superficial wounds, and he's certainly not just a skeleton. Likewise, in the book, Louella's head is described as gushing blood, and Haymitch is described as being soaked in it.

As with Ampert, though, in the movie, Louella has injuries, but they are far from gruesome. Perhaps the most notable change in this vein, however, is the fact that Silka decapitates Wellie and holds up her head in the novel. In the movie, Silka kills her, but it is absolutely nothing like this gruesome scene in the book. On the whole, it seems the movie wanted to make the movie more approriate for younger audiences, but that's a true letdown, not only because it goes against what the franchise is meant to show but also because it's frankly essential to The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping.

#3590. Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’

In 1972, Walter Hill was a young screenwriter with just one produced movie (“Hickey & Boggs”) behind him when he scored an enviable gig: adapting Jim Thompson’s tough-as-nails crime novel “The Getaway” for actor/producer Steve McQueen (then one of the biggest movie stars in the world) and director Sam Peckinpah (then, as now, one of the greatest directors who ever lived). On Wednesday night, Hill spoke before a packed screening at the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and looked back on the movie that jump-started not only his screenwriting endeavors, but a directing career that would ultimately include classics like “The Warriors,” “48hrs.,” and “Streets of Fire.” Related Stories Short Film ‘Lightning Bug’ Gives Stage and Screen Legend Lois Smith One of Her Greatest Roles — Watch It Here Is A24 Finally Big Enough to Be Considered a Major Studio?

“The Getaway” screened as part of the museum’s “Branch Selects” series, in which the Academy’s various branches program films they feel exemplify their crafts. “The Getaway” was, appropriately enough, selected by the writers branch, and screenwriter and Academy Governor Larry Karaszewski was on hand to introduce the movie and moderate the pre-screening discussion with Hill. Karaszewski, a longtime “Getaway” enthusiast who carried newspaper ads from the movie around in his wallet when he was 10 years old, pointed out that Hill changed the entire architecture of screenwriting when he burst onto the scene in the early 1970s.

“ Walter, right off the bat, changed the art of screenwriting,” Karaszewski said. “We have an award show here at the Oscars called the Sci-Tech Awards, where they give awards to things that silently change the industry and advance them into the future. I really feel that Walter Hill did that in screenwriting, but it wasn’t a technical advancement. It was a literary advancement. He changed what a page should look like as a screenplay and what it could feel like to read it.” Karaszewski went on to illustrate his point by projecting pages from Robert Bolt’s “Doctor Zhivago” screenplay and Walter Hill’s “Hard Times” side by side on the screen.

“You don’t even have to read [Bolt’s script], just look at it,” Karaszewski said, pointing out the dense blocks of words compared to Hill’s lean, spare page. “You’re looking at monoliths. It’s dense, and there are camera moves and references to things you would never see on screen. Walter Hill taught screenwriters that you can strip all that away. You can still direct on the page, but not by calling for specific camera movements — just by saying what you’re seeing. Walter’s scripts are made out of short sentences and white space. He looked at the placement of each line as part of the storytelling. He turned the carriage return into an art form.”

As Karaszewski welcomed Hill to the stage, he pointed out that “The Getaway” — a smart, terse tale of a couple (Steve McQueen and Ali MacGraw) on the run after their involvement in a botched bank robbery — represented the emergence of Hill’s developing voice. “You’ll already see the beginnings of that remarkable style, the economy, the precision, the sense that every line is pushing you toward the next image.” Yet, as Hill revealed in his lively conversation with Karaszewski, the ruthless efficiency of the pacing and the concentrated emotional impact of “The Getaway” were not easily arrived at.

“I think it’s much harder to adapt than it is to write an original, which is the reverse of the normal theory,” Hill said. “With an original, it’s just you at your desk with the typewriter or pen. When you’re adapting, that almost always means that somebody else owns it, so you’re not simply writing based on your own opinions about what should be in and what should be out, but there’s the producer’s opinion, and the studio’s, and the actor’s. There were all these political currents that one had to navigate.”

One such political current came from megastar McQueen, who didn’t interfere much with Hill’s writing but did have one caveat that amused the screenwriter. “He wanted to play a reasonably sympathetic outlaw,” Hill said. “That was not in the Thompson sensibility. So we already had a disparity, but the producer wanted to keep Steve happy.”

“The Getaway” began as an assignment not for Peckinpah, but for Peter Bogdanovich, who was white-hot coming off of successes like “The Last Picture Show” and “What’s Up, Doc?” Bogdanovich didn’t last long, however, given his clashes with McQueen and McQueen’s power as the film‘s star. “I couldn’t imagine two more diverse sensibilities than Steve and Peter,” Hill said, noting that he had his own disagreements with Bogdanovich over the movie’s tone but wasn’t in a position to argue. “You’ve got to remember, I was nobody. I had one screen credit. And these were big players.”

The big players included not only Bogdanovich and McQueen, but MacGraw, hot off of the smash hit “Love Story.” MacGraw was pushed into the movie by her husband, Paramount studio chief Robert Evans, which Hill found amusing given the way everything played out. “I’m going to tread lightly here,” Hill said of the behind-the-scenes melodrama involving MacGraw leaving Evans when she fell in love with McQueen. “When the material was optioned and I was hired, Bob saw the movie as a fabulous idea for Steve and Ali. It didn’t work out so well for him.”

After Bogdanovich and McQueen butted heads, Bogdanovich was let go and Peckinpah, who McQueen had enjoyed working with on “Junior Bonner,” came in to take his place. “We were very lucky to get such a talented guy, obviously,” Hill said. “I thought of him then and I think of him now as one of the great directors with a very unique sensibility. I was very privileged to work with him — which doesn’t mean he and I agreed about everything.”

Hill’s biggest disagreement with Peckinpah had to do with a scene in which MacGraw’s character considered killing McQueen before turning the gun on his nemesis — and the man with whom MacGraw had gone to bed to secure McQueen’s early release from prison. This was a scene carried over from the book, which was darker and more paranoid than what made it to the screen given McQueen’s mandate that he be sympathetic. Hill felt that the moment no longer worked now that the relationship between McQueen and MacGraw was softer and more relatable in the novel.

“I thought that for the movie we were trying to make, you might forgive your wife for sleeping with a bad man to do a very good thing for you,” Hill said. “That seemed to be to be conceivable. But if your wife fell into cahoots with the bad guy and actually was thinking about killing you and actually turned the gun on you before she decided to shoot the other guy…this did not track for me. But this is the screenwriter’s dilemma: you either talk the director into your point of view, or you make the change that he wants — or somebody else will. Those are your choices.”

Hill lost the argument but liked the movie Peckinpah made in the end. “He staged it beautifully,” Hill said. “He shot it beautifully. It’s got one of Steve’s best performances. And the movie turned out to be his greatest hit. He used to call me every once in a while after I became a director and say, ‘Write me another one.'” Ironically, it was the success of “The Getaway” that put Hill in a position where didn’t have to write for other directors anymore.

“Larry Gordon had a producing deal to make low-budget movies at Columbia,” Hill said. “He would give young writers a chance to direct, because he said, ‘Even if they’re no good as directors, at least we’ll get a good script. Most of the directors I’m working with aren’t any good anyway.'” Gordon gave Hill the opportunity to direct “Hard Times,” and the rest was history. Aside from kicking off Hill’s directing career, the collaboration became the first of many between the two men. “He’s a wonderful guy and a wonderful producer.”

Now in his 80s, Hill continues to write and direct (his last film was the exquisite character-driven Western “Dead for a Dollar“), plying his trade in the world of graphic novels in between film projects. “I’ve had four of them published in France,” Hill said, joking that the only one published in America was “the least good of them,” but promising another one on the way. “You’ve got to keep your hand in somehow.”

For information on Academy Museum programs, visit their website.

#3589. 'Ghost Accounts' Are Putting Your Security at Risk, but You Can Protect Yourself

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

In all the years you've been online, you've likely created more accounts than you can remember, whether to shop on a website you made one purchase from, sign up for a newsletter you've since stopped reading, or download apps for school or work that you no longer need.

These so-called "ghost accounts"—all the old, forgotten logins that are still active but not in use—could expose your data in the event of a breach, increasing the risk of your information being used in malicious ways. That's why it's important to go through the effort to find and delete dormant accounts. Here's how to get started.

As McAfee describes, ghost accounts may retain lots of sensitive data, such as your contact details (phone numbers, emails, and addresses), purchase histories, payment details, and passwords. While this doesn't mean your information is sure to be compromised, the more places it lives, the more opportunities there are for bad actors to get ahold of it.

You're less likely to be keeping tabs on activity in older accounts, which may also have weak or reused passwords that haven't been updated in years. If that company or service experiences a data breach, not only is your stored data there exposed, but that information (including your password) can be used to access other accounts using tactics like credential stuffing and phishing. This also increases the risk of identity theft, as threat actors can use your name, birth date, and other information to open fraudulent accounts.

Unfortunately, finding and removing forgotten accounts can be tedious. If you have a password manager, the easiest way to start is to audit older items as well as look at security reports that identify weak or reused passwords, as well as data breaches that have impacted your accounts. If you've saved credentials in your browser keychain, go through the same process to find dormant accounts.

The next place to look is in your email: Search for account confirmation and verification emails as well as password resets using keywords like "verify your email," "free trial," "welcome," "confirm your account," or "sign up." Add a date filter to narrow down older accounts. Do this across all of your email addresses.

Once you've found accounts you no longer use, the next step is to deactivate or delete them, which you may be able to do through the settings or by reaching out to customer support. At the very least, remove all identifying information and change the password, and if possible, update the address to a burner using your browser's or password manager's hide-my-email feature. If you no longer have access to an old account, that doesn't mean it's been deactivated and your information removed, so you may need to reach out to customer support to find out how to access and delete it.

#3588. ‘Josephine’ Review: Another Heartsick Horror Film About Real Monsters from ‘Soft & Quiet’ Filmmaker

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on January 23, 2026 during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Sumerian Pictures will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20, with a wide release to follow on Friday, December 4.]

At this point, filmmaker Beth de Araújo is two for two. Not just in terms of the quality of her films — impeccably crafted fever dreams of very different stripes and horrifyingly similar themes — but in how these films make the viewer feel.

More concisely: with her “Soft & Quiet” and “Josephine,” de Araújo remains undefeated when it comes to making stunning films that I will both heartily recommend and never, ever watch again. Related Stories Walter Hill on Sam Peckinpah, Steve McQueen, and His Revolutionary Screenplay for ‘The Getaway’ Short Film ‘Lightning Bug’ Gives Stage and Screen Legend Lois Smith One of Her Greatest Roles — Watch It Here

The word that comes to mind when watching a de Araújo feature is heartsick. That applies to the feeling bestowed on both the audience and her characters (the good guys and the bad guys). While her first film, the unrelenting “Soft & Quiet,” was cleverly designed to appear as if it was shot in a single real-time take, her sophomore feature is more about the steady accumulation of dread. The heroines of “Soft & Quiet” recognize what they are dealing with almost immediately (the force of the evil that is bent on destroying them is what’s surprises most), but the star at the center of “Josephine” is not just wounded by the sickness that suddenly infiltrates her young life, but her complete lack of understanding about what is happening to her and why.

In both films, it’s not just bad deeds that upends everyday lives, it’s real evil, actual monsters, perversions that don’t only show up in a movie screen. That’s true terror.

Based loosely on an experience de Araújo, who both wrote and directed the film, experienced as a child, “Josephine” initially lulls us into a false sense of safety. It’s early morning in San Francisco, and fledgling soccer star Josephine (Mason Reeves, riveting in her first role) is getting ready for a run with her devoted dad Damien (Channing Tatum, bringing incredible girl-dad energy to the role). It’s something the pair do every Sunday morning: get up early to watch Premier League football, run through a woodsy neighboring park, and kick the ball around.

For her second film, de Araújo leans less on clever camera tricks, though she and cinematographer Greta Zozula occasionally put us in Josephine’s own perspective, shooting as if we are looking through the eight-year-old’s eyes. As with “Soft & Quiet,” the gimmick works, grounding us in Josephine’s world and immersing us, if briefly, in what the world looks like from her vantage. Jo-Jo, as her dad calls her, is plucky and fun and filled with energy, so when she briefly zips ahead of her dad while on their run through Golden Gate Park, it just seems like everyday high-jinks.

But when the path forks (about as heavy-handed a metaphor as de Araújo will ever employ), Josephine goes to the left, while Damien goes to the right. What she finds there will forever alter the course of her life, and set “Josephine” off on a heart-wrenching journey with no easy answers. Curious and watchful, Josephine ducks behind a tree when she sees a woman (Syra McCarthy) running into a public bathroom at the bottom of a scrubby hill, and she sinks even further down when a young man (a bone-chilling Philip Ettinger) follows the unknown woman into the tiny building.

De Araújo’s approach to portraying on-screen violence only furthers that heartsick feeling: straightforward, unsparing, and absolutely devoid of any possibility of being compared to “torture porn.” What we see, what Josephine sees, is something no person should ever witness or experience. And that’s the root of the film’s power: how do we talk about things that we should not have words for?

When Damien arrives on the scene, it kicks off what will become one of Tatum’s best performances yet, a deep-feeling and heartbreaking exploration of layers of emotional unease. Damien does everything “right,” ensuring both Josephine and the woman are safe, chasing after the assailant, calling the cops, a neat little checklist of “how to handle an emergency.” And yet, the damage has already been done. There will be more to come.

Even when Josephine begins to seek out answers to what she’s seen (snatching her mom’s phone to search “raip,” reeling at what she discovers), it’s impossible to make sense of everything. There are things to fear she never even know existed, and the deep-seated powerlessness that overtakes her causes her to act out in chilling and increasingly volatile ways. Her parents’ reactions don’t help: her exceedingly calm mother Claire (Gemma Chan, thrilling as a character just barely holding it together) wants her to see a therapist now, her more action-oriented dad is eager to put her into self-defense classes. The mixed messages both give off (to say nothing of their own barely concealed terror) do little to help Josephine, who soon becomes someone almost entirely different than the care-free kid she just was.

She also picks up a new friend: Ettinger begins to appear to her, a literal haunting figure, never saying a word, yet barging into nearly every moment of Josephine’s already upended life. It’s the sort of choice another filmmaker fight fill tricksy or silly, but that de Araújo delivers with the maximum of impact. And that we, like Josephine and only Josephine, can see him only furthers our immersion into her world. It almost goes beyond empathy.

Josephine’s steadily unfolding breakdown is only compounded by the arrival of yet another situation no eight-year-old should ever have to encounter: handling the messy investigation of the crime itself. How she might help (or not) drives one more wedge between Josephine and her parents, who all have a different take on what the “right” thing to do is.

If these questions sound heady and heavy, they are, but de Araújo’s masterful ability to interrogate tension on every level keeps the film clipping along, each turn both a surprise and an inevitability. The monsters are here, they are real, and they’re coming.

“Josephine” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival.

#3586. Every Version of 'A Christmas Carol,' Ranked (and Where to Stream Them)

Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol is the greatest story about Christmas ever written—even better than the one with Mary and Joseph and the manger. The 1843 tale of a miser browbeaten by self-righteous ghosts is (probably) the most filmed story of all time. Dozens of cinematic adaptations of A Christmas Carol have been released in theaters and on TV since Scrooge; or Marley's Ghost came out in 1901. Hundreds or thousands if you count re-imaginings and very special episodes of sitcoms. But which version is the very best?

I've carefully considered every major theatrical and TV adaptation of A Christmas Carol and rated each in terms of holiday spirit, Dickensian whimsy, and Scrooge-osity to arrive at the definite, no-argument-possible best-to-worst list of Christmas Carols.

To rank Christmas Carols, you have to decide what A Christmas Carol is to you. My criteria for inclusion: It has to be full-length (at least around an hour long); it has to have been released widely, either in theaters, on network television, or through a larger streaming service, and it has to be fairly close to a direct adaptation—modernizations, re-imaginings, sequels, and that episode of The Six Million Dollar Man don’t count (sorry, Scrooged fans). Using those criteria, I’ve winnowed the Carols down to the 17 you see below, ranked from best to worst, along with where you can stream each one.

It's tough to pick a single adaptation of A Christmas Carol as the absolute best of all time, but the 1984 TV movie version starring George C. Scott is unassailable. Other versions do some things better, but this one does everything right—no mistakes. It stays close to the original text; it's perfectly produced; and it has a consistency of tone and vision that makes it the most balanced of all versions of the story. A Christmas Carol might not have the best Scrooge of all time, but George C. Scott's performance is a solid nine out of ten, and this version features the most adorable and pitiable Tiny Tim of all and the best Ghost of Christmas Present, played by Edward Woodward, who played the policeman in The Wicker Man.

Shot in the midst of the Great Depression, the first sound version of A Christmas Carol digs deeper into the despair and horror of the story than any other adaptation. It’s a bleak, German expressionist Christmas flick, and Seymour Hicks’ sickly, haunted portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge fits the tone perfectly. Instead of delighting in his own crapulence, Hicks plays Scrooge like Satan in The Divine Comedy—he's not the ruler of Hell; he's its most tormented prisoner. Scrooge's miserliness is played as pathology. He wears dirty, torn clothing and shivers miserably while eating gruel because he can’t bring himself to burn a single scrap of coal. Even when he converts, it seems like a manic episode instead of Christmas spirit, suggesting this could be a story about an old man going mad.

Where to stream: Sadly, the version on free streaming services like Tubi and Plex is colorized, but you can watch it on YouTube in glorious black and white.

This big-budget musical take on the Yuletide classic turns Dickens up to 11. Scrooge is huge, a raucous, crowd-pleasing musical with hundreds of extras, elaborate sets, and a scenery-chewing central performance from Albert Finney to hold it all together. But Finney and company also manage to keep the emotional core of the story intact. The music is great, with memorable tunes like “I Hate People,” a song that Finney snarls instead of sings. Scrooge has the best ghosts of any version of A Christmas Carol, too—you can't beat the cheesy awesomeness of big-money 1970s special effects.

Before Hallmark devoted its corporate life to forgettable holiday-themed romantic comedies, it co-produced one of the best versions of A Christmas Carol ever made. This entire movie belongs to Patrick Stewart, whose nuanced, layered portrayal of Scrooge is the best that has ever been done. His "conversion" scene is so visceral and honest, it brought a tear to my eyes, even though I've seen the exact scene performed in at least 40 other movies, stage plays, and episodes of 1980s sitcoms. Sadly, the paucity of basic cable budgets in the 1990s results in some chintzy-looking sets and laughable special effects that mar an otherwise top-notch production.

Horror director Ti West's Carol adaptation muddies the moral clarity of Dickens' tale and suggests there's something deeply troubling beneath all the Victorian holiday catharsis. With a few exceptions, Ebenezer hits the familiar beats of A Christmas Carol: It delivers the crowd-pleasing rich-jerk-turns-good story moviegoers expect, but West layers in subtle hints along the way that suggest the floorboards are rotten, and if you dance with Christmas joy too hard, you'll fall into the dark basement below. Ebenezer seems to whisper to audiences, "How much does the conversion of one miserly wretch matter in the face of systemic injustice? And isn't he going to snap out of it when the fright wears off anyway?" Bonus: As you'd probably expect from a Ti West movie, the ghosts are genuinely scary.

I'm sticking A Muppet Christmas Carol randomly here on the list because you can't reasonably compare it to other versions of the story. The Muppet version is a thing unto itself. Like the Ol' Dirty Bastard, its style has no father. A Muppet Christmas Carol is absolutely delightful from start to finish, for children, grown-ups, cats, dogs, space aliens, and anything else you got. It shouldn't even work to set Michael Caine's serious portrayal of Ebenezer Scrooge against a supporting cast of puppets, but somehow it all seems natural.

Alastair Sim takes Ebenezer Scrooge on a real journey in this movie. In the first act, he plays Scrooge like Capitalism personified, an uncaring, amoral monument to pure acquisition. He seems like a Scrooge who'd scare away ghosts, but when Marley shows up dragging his trademark chains, Sim is instantly reduced to pop-eyed fear, like the single chink in his armor is the supernatural. Scrooge then regresses to a childlike, bashful figure as ghosts lead him to different visions, finally emerging from his symbolic death to his rebirth as a Christmas-obsessed guy who lives to serve others. This movie might be among the best of the genre, but an unnecessary subplot about Scrooge's business sandbags the movie through part of the second act.

Mr. Magoo's Christmas Carol was the first animated version of A Christmas Carol and the first animated holiday special ever shown on American TV. The main character, Mr. Magoo, was the star of a one-joke, limited-animation cartoon popular in the early 1960s about an old man who couldn’t see very well, so it’s surprising how carefully crafted and effective this version of A Christmas Carol is. It's weirdly meta too: Jim Backus voices Mr. Magoo, who is a (blind) actor performing as Scrooge in A Christmas Carol on Broadway, so the play is bookended with "this guy can't see!" bits. The songs are strange, memorable and funny (listen to "Razzleberry Dressing" above once and you'll never forget it), but the emotional core of the story remains surprisingly powerful. Jim Backus is amazing.

I'm breaking my own rule about not including shortened versions of the story because this animated Carol is that great. Its evocative, graceful, hand-drawn look belongs to animation legend Richard Williams and was inspired by the illustrations from the original version of A Christmas Carol. It's a cartoon, but it's not a kiddie cartoon, so the darkness of the ghosts isn't glossed over. Plus, Scrooge is voiced by Alastair Sim, reprising his role from 1951's Scrooge.

There's nothing wrong with this brightly lit, by-the-numbers take on A Christmas Carol, but it seems designed to appeal to as broad an audience as possible, so the rough edges of the story have been sanded off. The ghosts aren’t that scary. Scrooge isn’t that miserly, etc. It’s fine for a Christmas movie to be lighthearted fun, but the lowered stakes ultimately blunt the emotional resonance of the climax, leading to a mediocre Christmas Carol.

I'm including this version of A Christmas Carol because it's Lifehacker editor Meghan Walbert's favorite. Sorry, Meghan, but this flimsy 1970s TV movie adaptation hasn't aged well. Henry Winkler does a good job as Scrooge, and it's cool to see Burgess Meredith and other old-timey stars, but overall, this is a schmaltzy, plodding film that unwisely replaces a lot of Dickens' best writing with the work of 1970s TV hacks.

Where to stream it: Pluto, Tubi, Amazon Prime

I really wanted to like Disney’s A Christmas Carol. Robert Zemeckis is a great director and Jim Carrey is a force of nature, but I couldn't get through it. There might be a lot to recommend this version of the story, but using 2009’s technology to create realistic-looking characters was such a puzzling choice. The whole movie looks like a video game cutscene from a PS3 game, and I kept wanting to hit “A” to skip ahead to the gameplay.

It doesn't seem like the producers of this obscure 2012 straight-to-streaming feature had much money to work with, which is too bad. If they had, they might have been able to better realize some of the intriguing ideas behind this movie. It's a straight-up horror take on the tale, but it just isn't scary. Sadly, you can't carry a feature film on good intentions. Overall, a swing and a miss.

The animation in this 1997 musical cartoon version of A Christmas Carol is dated, pedestrian, and ugly. The songs are forgettable, and Scrooge has a pet bulldog for some reason. (The one good joke is that he named his dog "Debit.") It’s just not good, which is a shame, because the cast is overflowing with talent, including Tim Curry as Scrooge, Ed Asner, and Whoopi Goldberg.

This BBC drama goes for a philosophical, moody version of Scrooge, but it doesn’t come together. It’s dark, grim, and so ponderously self-serious that it collapses under its own weight. In an effort to present aspects of A Christmas Carol that haven't been seen before (like "How Marley got his chains"), A Christmas Carol rewrites the original text from the ground up, but it comes across like Dickens' first draft with a bad case of Surf Dracula.

The current state of Dickens adaptation is not good. Netflix's uninspired, sappy, CGI version of A Christmas Carol tries to tart the story up with slapstick, songs, and jokes, but it’s all cynical, lowest-common-denominator horseshit. The dialogue has been dumbed down and joked up. Scrooge has a silly dog for comic relief. They added scatological humor. Think about this: The minds behind Scrooge: A Christmas Carol read Dickens and concluded, “This story would be better with a wacky dog and fart jokes.”

A Christmas Carol is such a solid story, even a grade-school production of it can be fun to watch. But a cynical production of it is extra terrible, given the message of the story. This terrible ego project is a bottom-of-the-barrel Christmas Carol because it feels like a money grab. Kelsey Grammer sucks as Scrooge, mugging his way through a lightweight performance. Jason Alexander sucks as Marley. Jennifer Love Hewitt is, well, actually pretty good as Scrooge’s Christmas-past romantic interest. She is a rare bright spot in this dreary movie, however. Everything else is mid to terrible. It’s shot and lit like a TV show; the sets are bland and the songs forgettable. Overall, it has the cynical feeling of assembly-line, “let’s get this shit over with” TV production.

#3585. The Witcher 4 Gets Official Update on Physical Release

'We’re nerds ourselves,' CD Projekt Red says

CD Projekt has confirmed that a physical version of The Witcher 4 will be released, even though the RPG is slated to launch after Sony Interactive Entertainment plans to stops producing physical games for PlayStation 5. Whether The Witcher 4 will be released on a physical disc is another matter entirely.

Sony plans to end the production of game discs for PlayStation consoles in January 2028. The Witcher 4 is the highest-profile AAA game currently slated to launch that year, and it comes from a studio that enjoys releasing its games physically. In an interview with The Game Business from August, CD Projekt joint CEO Michał Nowakowski confirmed that CD Projekt would still like to release a physical version of The Witcher 4.

"We’re big fans of people having access to tangible collectible things. We’re nerds ourselves, and we like that. We always supported that," Nowakowski explained. "So, whatever is the case, we’re going to be for sure having a box. We’re going to have a box that’s going to have some feelies in it. Something you’re going to be wanting to open up and enjoy."

That said, Nowakowski said he's unsure whether the game itself will be on a disc, as CD Projekt has no control over what Sony decides to manufacture. "We know what PlayStation has announced. And we have no influence on the policies of the first parties," he admitted. "The discs for the first parties, including PlayStation, have to be manufactured in their own factories. So, if they stop manufacturing indeed by 2028, then yes [we won’t have a disc]."

Although Nowakowski went on to tell The Game Business that he has "no influence" over whether it'll even be possible to print discs for The Witcher 4, it's good that CD Projekt is committing to a physical release regardless. That said, it's clear that PlayStation needs to better explain its plans to developers, some of whom are clearly still expressing demand for physical discs.

The Witcher 4 will be released on PS5, Windows PC, and Xbox Series X sometime in 2028. Before then, fans of the series can look forward to a current-generation remaster of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt on Sept. 29 and the Songs of the Past expansion for that game sometime in 2027.

#3584. Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $21 Million in Previews, Second-Best Result of 2026

““The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” earned $21 million in Thursday previews and early screenings on Wednesday and is expected to dominate the box office this weekend. Analysts believe it will earn north of $100 million. The preview figures are the second-best of 2026, behind “Spider-Man: Brand New Day’s” massive $72 million haul. It’s also the second-best for the “Hunger Games” franchise, just behind the $25.5 million that “Catching Fire” earned in 2013. It’s a big improvement on the last “Hunger Games” prequel, “The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes,” which made $5.75 million in previews and kicked off with $44 million. That film would gross over $166 million domestically and nearly $364 million globally, figures that “Sunrise on the Reaping” is on pace to easily eclipse.

“Sunrise on the Reaping” is based on Suzanne Collins’ bestselling novel of the same name. It tells the origin story of Haymitch Abernathy, the alcoholic former Hunger Games victor played by Woody Harrelson in the films. The sequel checks in with him at 16 as he’s forced to compete in gladiatorial combat. “East of Eden” breakout Joseph Zada plays Haymitch. He’s surrounded by an all-star cast that includes Jesse Plemons, Ralph Fiennes, Glenn Close, Kieran Culkin, Elle Fanning, Mckenna Grace, and Maya Hawke. Francis Lawrence, who helmed most of the series’ films, returns as director. Lionsgate, which is having a strong year at the box office thanks to “Michael,” is backing the “Hunger Games” sequel as it has the previous films.

The biggest competition for “Sunrise on the Reaping” this weekend isn’t another major movie, but the release of “Grand Theft Auto 6,” which is expected to be a phenomenon.

#3583. 10 Most Iconic Archie Comics Stories of All Time

For more than eight decades, the fictional town of Riverdale has been America’s quintessential backdrop for teen and pop culture, outlasting even the most iconic comic book franchises. What began in 1941 as a lighthearted showcase of malt-shop mishaps and high school rivalries evolved into a sandbox of stories that has stayed endlessly recognisable ever since.

Much of that longevity comes from Archie Comics’ willingness to take risks. Rather than relying solely on slapstick comedy, the publisher used its characters to address real-world social issues, lead bizarre genre crossovers, and eventually dismantle its own squeaky-clean image. Moving from zombie apocalypses to more grounded stories, few comic book universes have a catalogue as varied or as culturally resilient.

Over its more than eighty-year publication history, Archie Comics has produced iconic stories that have not only stood the test of time but also rank among the best the medium has to offer. This article highlights 10 of the most iconic Archie Comics stories of all time, representing the absolute highlights of its legacy.

Archie vs. Predator delivered one of pop culture’s wildest tonal collisions by pitting Riverdale’s cheerful teens against cinema’s deadliest extraterrestrial hunter. Released in April 2015 and written by Alex de Campi, the four-issue miniseries begins with an idyllic spring break trip where Betty and Veronica accidentally attract a ruthless Yautja warrior back home.

The story doesn’t shy away from the predator’s lethal brutality as he kills several armed people while hunting Veronica. The series gleefully unleashes full-blown R-rated slasher carnage across Riverdale’s bright, nostalgic aesthetic, systematically slaughtering beloved supporting characters in hilariously gruesome fashion. Its willingness to embrace its premise made it an instant cult phenomenon,

Archie #1 sees Mark Waid and Fiona Staples reimagine one of comics’ most enduring characters, ushering Riverdale into the modern era after seventy-five years of continuity. The relaunch traded classic house-style gag strips for a grounded, serialised teen dramedy, opening with a mysterious fallout known simply as "the Lipstick Incident" that fractures Archie and Betty’s lifelong romance.

Waid and Staples turned Riverdale’s teens into complex, relatable modern adolescents, marking a milestone for the company by reintroducing the characters in a way that felt fresh yet familiar. The new look and design suited a new generation of readers and offered a welcome change of pace for lifelong fans.

Chilling Adventures of Sabrina was published by Archie Horror, an imprint of Archie Comics, and offers a darker take on Sabrina the Teenage Witch. Written by Roberto Aguirre-Sacasa with artwork by Robert Hack, the series follows sixteen-year-old Sabrina Spellman as her upcoming Dark Baptism forces her to make an agonising choice between her mortal boyfriend and her sinister coven.

Steeped in gothic dread, satanic rituals, and genuine psychological terror, the comic stripped away every trace of sitcom whimsy to create an unsettling folk-horror masterpiece. Chilling Adventures of Sabrina became a major critical sensation, inspiring a loose television adaptation of the same name that ran for four parts and 36 episodes.

Published in July 2014, Life with Archie #36 delivered one of the most shocking moments in modern comic history by killing off Riverdale’s eternal everyman, Archie Andrews. This was the second-to-last issue in the series, bringing a melancholic close to the adult timelines where Archie married Betty and Veronica.

Archie dies after foiling an assassination attempt at Pop’s Chock’lit Shoppe that targeted Senator Kevin Keller’s life. Archie heroically dove into the line of fire and took a fatal bullet to the abdomen. His dying words to Betty and Veronica were “I’ve always loved you”. Archie dies protecting a friend, providing a fitting end and farewell to the selfless character.

Afterlife with Archie shattered every wholesome expectation surrounding Riverdale by plunging its iconic teenagers into a visceral zombie apocalypse. The series begins when Sabrina Spellman uses forbidden dark magic to bring Jughead’s beloved dog, Hot Dog, back to life. This act inadvertently unleashes an unstoppable undead plague across town.

The book earned widespread praise for embracing horror elements rather than the bright coloured panels the franchise was familiar with, and for treating Riverdale’s cast with brutal emotional stakes. Afterlife with Archie proved so wildly successful that it launched the Archie Horror imprint and directly paved the way for the dark, genre-bending reinvention of television’s Riverdale.

The Archieverse was forever changed with the debut of Kevin Keller, who is the first LGBT+ character in Archie Comics history. The fan-favourite character made his debut in Veronica #202, inadvertently making it one of the most sought-after comics in the franchise's history, selling out upon its initial release.

The issue opens with Veronica immediately falling head over heels for the new handsome transfer student, unaware that Kevin has no romantic interest in her or any girl at Riverdale High, completely subverting expectations. The story handles Kevin's sexuality tactfully, integrating him into Riverdale’s lighthearted rhythm through effortless comedy as Jughead helps Kevin navigate Veronica’s relentless, misguided romantic schemes.

Archie Marries Veronica / Archie Marries Betty finally answered the franchise’s oldest question through two distinct alternate futures. Written by Michael Uslan, the ambitious six-part arc was originally presented in Archie #600-605. Issues #600-602 present a story set in an alternate future where Archie, after his college graduation decides to marry Veronica Lodge.

In Issues #603-605, he chooses to marry Betty Cooper instead of Veronica. It treats both possible marriages with deep emotional maturity, elevating Riverdale’s familiar characters into complex adults with realistic struggles and lingering regrets. The event was an immediate hit, selling out shops nationwide and inspiring the acclaimed Life with Archie series that followed.

Love Showdown is a four-part comic book story arc released in 1994, featuring Archie Comics characters and finally tackling Riverdale’s most famous romantic stalemate head-on. The famous love triangle between Archie, Betty, and Veronica was supposedly put to an end in this comic, making it one of the most iconic moments in Archie Comics history.

The story kicks off with Archie receiving a mysterious love letter. Both Betty and Veronica inevitably think the other sent it due to Reggie’s meddling. This caused the girls to compete for Archie’s affection, urging him to choose between them once and for all. This leads to a moment where Betty upstages Veronica at a popular dance.

Nonetheless, it was ultimately revealed that the one who sent the letter was neither of them and none other than Cheryl Blossom, a girl from Archie’s past. At the end of the story, Archie unexpectedly chose Cheryl instead of the two. Archie’s Love Showdown Special would later bring the love triangle back to its former status quo.

Published in 1994, Archie Meets the Punisher is one of the most improbable crossovers in comic book history. Written by Batton Lash, with artwork by John Buscema and Stan Goldberg, the legendary one-shot brings together Marvel’s ruthless, gun-toting vigilante Frank Castle and Riverdale’s wholesome, milkshake-sipping teenagers, creating an unforgettable pop-culture fever dream that somehow works brilliantly.

The absurd premise centres on mistaken identity: a drug dealer named Red, who looks like Archie Andrews, flees to Riverdale to evade Castle’s relentless pursuit. As the Punisher stalks the quiet town’s high school hallways and sock hops, Archie and his friends are caught in the middle of lethal organised crime when thugs from New York arrive searching for Red.

The story plays the wildly contrasting tones of the two franchises completely straight, making it instantly iconic and entertaining. It also allowed Buscema’s gritty realism and Goldberg’s classic house style to share panels effortlessly. Archie Meets the Punisher shattered boundaries for inter-company crossovers, paving the way for other wild encounters in Riverdale, like those with KISS and the Predator.

Released in 1941, Pep Comics #22 quietly altered comic book history by introducing a clumsy, red-headed teenager named Archie Andrews, as well as Jughead and Betty, who would become fan favourite characters. This comic went against the grain and proved that everyday adolescent misadventures, high school crushes, and relatable neighbourhood humour could captivate young readers nationwide.

In this story, Archie “Chick” Andrews, desperate to impress his new neighbour, Betty Cooper, chose to walk on a fence blindfolded, but this death-defying stunt ends in disaster. He inevitably falls and destroys Betty’s father’s painting and her mother’s vase in the process. As recompense, he becomes Betty’s assistant at the taffy stand at a carnival.

Unfortunately, Betty gets him as a replacement for the tightrope walker, and it all ends with him falling into the taffy machine, spilling its contents all over Mr Cooper. The cultural impact of this comic cannot be overstated, leading to Archie getting his own solo title and the entire publisher being rebranded as Archie Comics.
