#3582. The Best Tech Deals From the Sam's Club Early Black Friday Sale

Retailers are churning out early Black Friday deals already, including the likes of Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and others. If you're waiting around for Friday, Nov. 27 to do all of your shopping, you might miss out on some deals and unnecessarily make the day more stressful than it needs to be. If you're a Sam's Club member, you have access to many early Black Friday deals worth checking out. I spent some time combing through their website and rounded up my favorite tech deals below.

The Bose SoundLink Flex SE is a portable Bluetooth speaker with an IP67 waterproof rating. The speaker even floats in the water, so you can bring it with you into the pool. While it doesn't offer full EQ customization in its companion app, the sound has rich bass depth and clear highs out of the box. It also features a speakerphone, allowing you to take calls and speak with it. It's light and portable, and the Bluetooth 5.3 supports multipoint connectivity and SBC, AAC, and aptX codecs. You can get the Bose 2nd Generation SoundLink Flex SE for $89 (originally $139).

Skullcandy makes fun speakers and headphones, although they're not designed for audiophiles (their sound signature is very bass-heavy). Their Skullcandy Stomp XL Max is their attempt at making a portable party speaker. It comes with two wireless mics, making it a great option for karaoke. It holds 12 hours of battery life (up to 20 hours with certain settings), has an IPX5 water resistance rating, and has LED lights that sync to the music. You can get it for $99 (originally $199).

Getting a soundbar can exponentially improve anyone's entertainment system, but a 5.1 system with rear speakers and a subwoofer takes it to the next level. The Samsung HW-Q65F 5.1 Channel Soundbar is $299 (originally $399), and it's a wireless setup that will keep the harmony of "too many cables" in the house. It supports Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X to give you a 3D audio feel, and it has a dialogue feature that will let you hear the whispers.

Gaming monitors can get expensive quickly, but you can get decent options on a budget. A great example is the 31.5-inch MSi gaming monitor selling for $129 (originally $179). It has a 250Hz refresh rate and a 1ms response time to make gaming smoother. There's also AMD FreeSync Premium to get rid of tearing and stuttering.

These kinds of sales are always a good time to upgrade laptops. If you're looking for a powerful computer that is well-rounded, consider the 16-inch HP OmniBook 7 Flip going for $699 (originally $899). This laptop comes with an Intel Ultra 5 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 16GB of RAM (which, honestly, is the minimum anyone should be buying in 2026).

If you need a bigger screen, the 17.3-inch HP OmniBook 3 is a good choice for a bit less money. It comes with an Intel Core Ultra 7 processor, 512GB of SSD, and 12GB of RAM. Part of the bigger screen means a bigger keyboard, so if you deal with numbers a lot, you'd likely appreciate the numeric pad.

If you want your laptop strictly for gaming, the ASUS TUF F16 Gaming laptop is $1,149 (originally $1,399). With an Intel Core 7 processor and the RTX 5060 graphics card, you'll be well set up to tackle heavy games. It comes with a 165Hz refresh rate, Advanced Arc Flow fans and vents to keep your machine cool, and 16GB DDR5 RAM to keep your loads short.

Budget TVs get big discounts during Black Friday, and the 58-inch Vizio QLED TV is one of them. You can get one for $178 (originally $298), and it supports Dolby Vision HDR for better color and contrast. The operating system is the Vizio OS, but of course, you can always change it with a TV dongle if you prefer a different one.

If you prefer to splurge for a better QLED but still get a good deal, the 65-inch Samsung QN90H QLED TV at $1,197.99 (originally $1,497.99) is a great option. It upscales lower-resolution pictures to 4K with AI. It works for gaming with its 144Hz refresh rate, and because the operating system is Tizen OS, it comes with Samsung TV Plus, which brings over 2,700 free channels. The TV also comes with Dolby Atmos, so you can hear audio with a 3D effect as the audio follows objects around the display.

A 100-inch TV makes a statement: You take your entertainment system seriously. The 100-inch Vizio QLED TV is a budget-friendly option with a $300 discount, currently going for $1,198 (originally $1,498). This TV supports Dolby Vision HDR for more vivid images and has hundreds of free channels with the Vizio OS.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

Black Friday sales officially begin Friday, November 27, 2026, and run throughout “Cyber Week,” the five-day period that runs from Thanksgiving through Cyber Monday,  November 30, 2026. But Black Friday and Cyber Monday dates have expanded as retailers compete for customers. You can get the same Black Friday sales early, and we expect sales to wind down by December 2, 2026.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that can be rare throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech. Of course, if you need to save money, the best way to save is not to buy anything.

#3581. ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance

[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on October 2, 2026 during the 2026 New York Film Festival. Janus Film will release the film in limited theaters on Friday, November 20.]

Paul Thomas Anderson‘s eye for vivifying music onscreen dates back to the late 1990s when, after “Boogie Nights,” he made Technicolor mini-masterpiece music videos with his ex-girlfriend Fiona Apple — or made a San Fernando Valley-sized shrine to Aimee Mann with his third feature, “Magnolia.” Since then, he’s kicked around with HAIM while turning one third of its Los Angelino triumvirate, Alana Haim, into a screen actress. He’s shot for Radiohead and made a regular collaboration with band member Jonny Greenwood to create some of the 21st century’s most memorable scores. Many young cinephiles now associate the mischievously lilty notes of “Phantom Thread” with the poison promise of new love and obsessive creation. Related Stories Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $21 Million in Previews, Second-Best Result of 2026 ‘Josephine’ Review: Another Heartsick Horror Film About Real Monsters from ‘Soft & Quiet’ Filmmaker

Last December, PTA teamed up with Geese frontman Cameron Winter to film, while operating his own Panavision camera, his solo stage performance at Carnegie Hall, running through sparse piano arrangements of tracks off his solo album, “Heavy Metal.” The result, a 72-minute film now being distributed roadshow-style by Janus Films before inevitably living on the Criterion Collection, is a stunning arrangement of its own: a deeply achey, sincere but never cloyingly earnest concert movie that’s tender to the point of frailty. (Benny Safdie counts as a co-producer, and the film’s scratchy New York quality and setting can’t help but have his imprint.)

The matted-hair, lithe Winter can seem a bit uncomfortable in his own skin in the public eye, as he did onstage ahead of “Cameron Winter at Carnegie” at its New York Film Festival world premiere at Alice Tully Hall. But on the piano, laser-beamed into his songcraft, he’s quietly electrified, at seemingly at peace as his tenorous vocal glissando and nimble fingerwork on the piano produce shiveringly tender folk ballads that echo Harry Nilsson and Van Morrison. (The usual comparisons to Tom Waits and Rufus Wainright are right, too, but Winter is his own strange thing.) If you weren’t previously sold on the wily Winter antic rock chaos of Geese — rapidly becoming one of the most popular contemporary art rock bands of these times — you’re about to. Paul Thomas Anderson has created a rhapsodic shrine to the man that is nonetheless ballad-sized in its emotional scale.

Winter, in December, played and sang to a sold-out crowd of more than 2,700 at the stately cultural temple that is Carnegie Hall, and this film can at times feel like a religious experience, an incantation, a lonely vigil. The singer/songwriter was 23 at the time of the performance, one year older than Bob Dylan when he headlined Carnegie Hall, and similarly at the precipice of major fame. Fixed on a mobile rig that will at times careen and whoosh across the stage when not otherwise holding on Winter, Anderson’s camera catches the expressionism and chiaroscuro of stage lights illuminating and fading off the singer’s face.

The result is hynoptic, a concert film up there with “Stop Making Sense” but for introverts. Songs like the popular single “$0” acquire an even more wrenchingly somber quality as a lovelorn protagonist rues being exploited by a relationship (“You’re making me feel like a dollar in your hand / You’re making me feel like I’m a zero dollar man”). Stripped of production, his indie hit “Love Takes Miles” plays even better. While many of the songs sort of hover in the same key and bleed into one another, that makes for an all the more transfixing experience. The lack of an interstitial anything save for a sweet prologue and moving coda make for experience also that’s immersive, deep, and the kind whose truth you can feel somewhere in your body even if you can’t quite articulate it.

“Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall premiered at the New York Film Festival. Janus Films will release it in theaters starting November 20.

#3580. Pokémon Go Pawniard Community Day event guide

Get yourself a shiny blue knight-samurai or two

Get yourself a shiny blue knight-samurai or two

Pokémon Go is having a Pawniard Community Day event on Saturday, Nov. 21 from 2-5 p.m. in your local time. This event is indeed running alongside the "Dynamax Trails" event, and it begins right when Eternatus' stint in the morning ends.

As expected with a Community Day event, Pawniward will spawn in huge numbers with a high chance for it to appear shiny. There are also several other bonuses and perks, which we've listed out below.

As per old research by the now-defunct website The Silph Road (via Wayback Machine), shiny rates on Community Days are about 1 in 24, which means that if you keep playing throughout the three-hour window, you should find quite a few shiny Pokémon.

If you’re short on time or Poké Balls, you can pop an Incense, then quickly tap each Pawniard to check for shiny ones, running from any that aren’t shiny. Notably, any Pawniard you’ve already tapped will face where your player is standing, so that should help identify which ones you may have already checked.

If you evolve Bisharp into Kingambit from 2-9 p.m. in your local time, it will learn the charged move Kowtow Cleave.

If you miss out on evolving it during this period, you will likely be able to evolve it during a Community Day weekend event in December to get Kowtow Cleave. If you don’t want to wait, you can use an Elite TM to get the move.

Usually, to evolve Bisharp into Kingambit, you'd need to set Bisharp as your buddy and beat 15 dark- or steel-type Pokémon in raids. However, for this Community Day, this requirement has been reduced heavily.

On Saturday, Nov. 21 from 2-9 p.m., you will only need to defeat 1 dark- or steel-type Pokémon in a raid with Bisharp as your buddy to evolve it into Kingambit. The evolution will still cost 100 Pawniard Candy, though. The Bisharp you are trying to evolve won't need to be used in the raid, it just needs to be set as your buddy Pokémon.

With its Community Day move, Kingambit is actually a very strong dark-type attacker, only falling to Mega and shadow Pokémon. Definitely power one up and give it Snarl and Kowtow Cleave for success.

Its Community Day move also makes it a strong pick in PvP, specifically in the Great League. Run it with Low Kick, Iron Head, and Kowtow Cleave to make the most of it.

The following bonuses will be active during Pawniard Community Day:

That said, you should definitely put your eggs in Incubators and pop an Incense and try to nab some powerful Pawniard.

If you can Mega Evolve Gyarados, Steelix, Scizor, Skarmory, Houndoom, Tyranitar, Sableye, Mawile, Aggron, Sharpedo, Absol, Metagross, Lucario, Greninja, or Malamar, you’ll score additional Pawniard Candy per catch.

Pokémon is celebrating its 30th anniversary and has partnered with many major brands. Now, another brand has partnered with this large Japanese franchise, featuring Tommy Lee Jones.

Jones is an award-winning actor who has appeared in numerous projects, including the Men in Black trilogy as Agent K, Volcano as Michael Roark, and, more recently, the FX series The Lowdown as Lee Raybon Sr. Outside his acting career, which began in 1969, Jones has also served as a spokesperson for Japanese beverage company Suntory, portraying a character known as "Alien Jones" in commercials for its BOSS coffee brand. Jones has played this character since 2006; he's described as an alien who takes human form to observe daily life on Earth, and he's appeared in numerous ads promoting the product, where he interacts with and watches the Japanese people in different scenarios, such as a school teacher and a police officer. On Suntory's social media channels, it has released a series of videos featuring Alien Jones investigating different Pokémon. The commercials are titled "BOSS Alien Jones Pokémon Investigation," where the sketched version of Alien Jones observes Psyduck, Magikarp, Ditto, and Wobbuffet. Meanwhile, on the official Suntory Japanese website, visitors will be greeted with Jones dressed up as Alien Jones, with Pikachu's tail and ears, with a translated quote of him saying, "I tried to become Pikachu. The Pokémon x BOSS Coffee collab began back in August 2026. Beyond images and videos of Jones dressing up and researching Pokémon, the brand will also release exclusive Pokémon-printed BOSS Coffee products, with cans featuring a Pokédex entry for Pikachu and other notable Pokémon, including the Gen 1 and Gen 8 starters. Additionally, buying a six-pack of BOSS Coffee gives fans a chance to win exclusive merchandise, such as T-shirts, notepads, and jackets, featuring both BOSS and Pokémon branding. The campaign is only available in Japan, but fans can still get involved, as it ends before December.

#3578. 10 Questions The Body Season 2 Still Needs To Answer

Shealyn Scott is a Senior Writer at Screen Rant. She has been writing for the site since 2024, focused on network, reality, streaming, and classic television. A creative writer, journalist, and lover of the written word in all its forms, Shealyn enjoys deconstructing scenes from her favorite shows, using context clues and historical precedent to predict major plot points (which, due to her successful track record, has sparked rumors of clairvoyance). As an award-winning student journalist, Shealyn spent her college years advocating for the humanities while studying English Literature. Her love of storytelling propelled her to expand her degree with minors in Writing and History, believing life to be a mere collection of stories that can be framed in as many ways as a movie scene. As a Senior member of the TV Team, Shealyn treats the series she covers like books, analyzing every line, camera angle, and lighting choice. Thankfully, her personal mission statement lines up perfectly with Screen Rant: every creative work deserves just as much thought from the viewer as it received from its creator.

This article contains discussion of religious trauma, drug overdose, and suicide.

The Body ended with a bang, but the hit coming-of-age drama left plenty of loose ends to tie up. Set in 2004 at a co-ed Catholic school in the Northeast United States, The Body follows the St. Mark's Lions, a high-octane dance team on the road to regionals. When a Halloween night hazing goes awry for the squad's newest member, however, the status quo is disrupted by a transfer student with potentially deadly ambition.

Between immense streaming success and a quickly-secured cult following, the smash-hit series is the latest addition to a new era of Netflix, characterized by thrilling stories with supernatural twists. Unsurprisingly, many viewers are already clamoring for The Body season 2, but the first eight episodes are filled to the brim with unresolved mysteries and burning questions that Netflix needs to answer.

From the very beginning, Lisbeth Anderson (Geena Meszaros) is desperate to join the Lions, though her dancing ability is nowhere near the level expected from the team. As such, when co-captain Anya Butler (Kristina Bogic) invites Lisbeth to the fateful Halloween party, the pair easily become partners in crime after Grace Franklin (Sofia Wylie) seemingly dies. For the bulk of the season, both girls keep their involvement a secret, only for everything to unravel in the final episode.

Whereas The Body season 1's ending sees Anya remorsefully confess to their cover-up, Lisbeth takes a different approach by telling her teammates she is the reason Grace came back from the dead. As her mother revealed earlier in the season, the cult Lisbeth grew up in hailed her as a healer, giving her the perfect backstory to manipulate the fairly gullible Lions. Yet, there's no telling whether Lisbeth's luck has run out or whether the team will fall under her spell once again due to their religious paranoia.

When Father Franklin (Nnamdi Asomugha) reveals that Grace has fallen into a minimally conscious state, the Lions immediately fear that it was somehow their fault. Slowly but surely, Lisbeth feeds into the panic by centering the narrative on the prank they played Halloween night: jokingly sacrificing Grace to Satan. While not every dancer was convinced they had actually communed with the Devil, the more impressionable students bought in quickly. The loudest contrarian, Elise Zakaria (Sara Boustany), decides to poke fun at them by staging a "vision" of Grace in the middle of mass.

Unexpectedly, her plan backfires as other Lions gradually pretend to see Grace themselves, save for Maddie Delaney (Shirley Chen). While The Body is forthcoming in stating the majority of the team faked their visions, Maddie— the only girl to honestly hold out— claimed she saw Grace during their performance at regionals. Similarly, Anya's visions of Grace were one of The Body's key thriller elements. As Elise posited, they could have been sleep-deprived hallucinations, but there's still a chance that Grace wasn't simply a manifestation of Anya's guilt.

Although the running assumption throughout The Body is that Grace either had a bad reaction to an ecstasy pill or was possessed by the Devil, the series never outright confirms what happened to her on Halloween night. The last time the viewer sees her as her normal self is when she wanders into the nearby woods, followed closely by Leo Anderson (Jackson Kelly) while Steven Maxwell (Orlando Norman) watches.

Before the twist ending of episode 1, it seemed like The Body was veering into murder mystery territory. Of course, the story changed once religious hysteria began to trickle in. Nevertheless, it's possible something happened to Grace before Anya and Lisbeth found her body. Granted, the show explicitly clears Leo, as he's the one who finds her unconscious later that night, but Steven makes a point throughout the season to mention that he blacked out on Halloween and has no recollection of his time spent with Grace.

Though the Andersons may not be the most dysfunctional family in film history, what we know about Lisbeth and Leo's upbringing is tragic. The children grew up in a religious fundamentalist group that their father led until his untimely demise. With the help of the Catholic Church, the two transfer to St. Mark's with their mother, Catherine (Louisa Krause).

Throughout The Body season 1, Catherine is an awful parent, with Lisbeth often having to act as both sister and mother to Leo. Via home videos, the viewer gets snippets of their life in West Virginia, but the true extent of Lisbeth and Leo's religious trauma remains to be seen. Likewise, it's suggested that Lisbeth may have been involved in her father's death, which would be a fascinating point to explore in season 2.

As the tongue-in-cheek title suggests, much of The Body is rooted in biblical horror. The motif is carried through nearly every aspect of the show, from the soundtrack to the set design. Yet, the most intriguing symbol is that of the snake, both literally and figuratively. When Lisbeth finds Grace's body in the woods, a snake appears to slither out of her hood. Similarly, on a snowy weekend retreat, Lisbeth wakes up to a snake under her blanket in the middle of the night.

Given her family's secret history of snake handling, Lisbeth accuses someone of messing with her, causing the group to suspect Elise, who is ostracized as the metaphorical snake of the team. Later, Anya and Elise discuss the possibility that Lisbeth planted the snake herself. While that's not unfathomable by any stretch of the imagination, The Body never shies away from showing the viewer every gritty detail of Lisbeth's schemes. Consequently, it doesn't make sense for the snake to be the one thing kept in the dark— unless, of course, it holds a deeper significance that season 2 can elaborate on.

Despite Grace and Leo initially seeming close, whatever friendship they had erodes when Grace looks through Leo's sketchbook and finds nude depictions of herself. The repressed teen boy explains that the drawings were meant to be an outlet for his "impure" thoughts, which makes it all the more interesting that each picture is modeled after an iconic religious artwork.

The Netflix thriller only shows a few sketches in full, but they seem to match the broad framework of the narrative, with Grace going from sacrificial lamb to a venerable saintlike figure over the course of the season. Maddie goes so far as to call him Grace's first apostle, so if there is a supernatural religious plot coming, Leo's sketchbook may reveal "Saint" Grace's true fate.

By the end of The Body season 1, Catherine has lost control of both her children. While she earnestly believes a holy reckoning is coming, Leo accepts Grace as his new deity, and Lisbeth seems completely disillusioned with spirituality as a whole.

After the teenagers diverge into their two distinct paths, Catherine stays home watching videos from their old church, specifically focusing on a sermon that claims they're immune to poison as long as they have faith. Sadly, it's implied that Catherine's religious delusion claims her life. With Lisbeth and Leo now orphaned, it's unclear what role—if any— they can play in season 2, unless a member of the community graciously takes them in.

In one of the most emotional scenes of the series, The Body's finale blows up Anya's relationships with Elise and Steven, which proves to be the final straw for the queen bee. As Lisbeth attempts to mastermind a new ruse at the debutante ball, Anya tearfully confesses to Father Franklin that she is a liar, cheater, and possible murderer.

Yet, Father Franklin may not have any reason to report her to the authorities. Despite Anya admitting to leaving a presumably dead body at the Franklin house on Halloween night, Grace wakes up before anyone can even call the police. With the young girl apparently back— and claiming to be God in the flesh— Anya's confession may have been in vain.

The Body set up numerous possibilities for Grace's death in episode 1, ranging from a snake bite to an overdose on ecstasy, but there was no explanation given for what happened after Lisbeth and Anya dropped off her corpse. Furthermore, everything that Grace experienced in the hospital— inexplicable seizures, miraculously breathing on her own, etc.— adds up to something science can't explain.

Netflix's smash-hit psychological drama The Body is full of complex characters, but some of the biggest players are more sympathetic than others.

Considering the camera took special care to show her ears during pivotal conversations, Grace could have heard everything that was said to and about her during her coma, inspiring the young girl to feed into her burgeoning sainthood. Some viewers even believe Grace faked the entire ordeal, which would both explain why the hospital's tests all came back normal and be a major twist that recontextualizes The Body's psychological drama.

To that end, The Body enjoys making the viewer question everything— including the genres it is categorized under. Despite the series being labeled as supernatural horror, there's an underlying skepticism baked into the narrative, as nearly every strange occurrence the main characters experience could be logically explained.

Regardless, The Body leaves just enough room for doubt to linger in the audience's minds. Be it Anya's so-called hallucinations, Grace surviving after her heart stops, or the countless little details meant to unnerve you, the drama delights in challenging you to separate the benign from the divine. Without question, The Body is designed to be enigmatic, but season 2 will have to decide whether the mass hysteria is truly groundless or if paranormal activity is haunting St. Mark's.

#3576. What ‘Digger’ Has in Common with Gary Oldman’s Winston Churchill and Charlize Theron’s Megyn Kelly

Tom Cruise‘s performance in Alejandro González Iñárritu‘s “Digger” is one of the boldest and most entertaining of the actor’s career, as he suppresses not only his usual movie star charisma but his entire way of walking and talking to play paunchy, aging oil tycoon Digger Rockwell. Cruise is barely recognizable in the role, which is about as far from heroic characters like Pete “Maverick” Mitchell and Ethan Hunt as Cruise’s Ron Kovic in “Born on the Fourth of July” was from race car driver Cole Trickle almost 40 years ago.

To aid in his complete transformation, Cruise called on one of the best prosthetic designers in the business, Kazu Hiro. Hiro has turned Gary Oldman into Winston Churchill (“The Darkest Hour”), Charlize Theron into Megyn Kelly (“Bombshell”), and Dwayne Johnson into “Smashing Machine” Mark Kerr, but transforming Cruise into Texas oilman Digger Rockwell was a whole new task — one made even more challenging by Iñárritu and Cruise’s persistent striving for perfectionism, and constant eagerness to try new approaches. Related Stories ‘Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall’ Review: PTA’s Spellbinding Concert Doc Is a Gorgeously Tender Performance Box Office: ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ Scores $21 Million in Previews, Second-Best Result of 2026

“Alejandro is an amazing director, and he has lots of ideas,” Hiro told IndieWire. “Every day he comes in with a new idea, and we have to come up with an answer for how to achieve it. And Tom is really professional, and expects everybody else to be at that same level, ready for any situation. After the first day of testing, I learned that I had to stay flexible to respond to whatever they wanted.”

To that end, Hiro created modular prosthetics whose parts could easily be swapped out and moved around, so that Cruise and Iñárritu could constantly try new looks. “Sometimes with heavy makeup, you can’t change it,” Hiro said. “I created prosthetics that could be mixed, so we could make new designs on the spot — try this forehead with these cheeks and this nose, then change it.” Creating Cruise’s look was a constantly evolving process throughout the long prep period. “We didn’t have a clear answer until the end of rehearsal.”

Hiro’s mandate at the beginning was a bit open-ended, which gave him room for artistic exploration but also made it difficult to zero in on a precise look. “Alejandro said the character was 76 years old and an oil tycoon,” Hiro said. “He also said he didn’t want the character to look like Tom, but he still wanted to see Tom in the character.” To try to find a concrete image for Digger Rockwell, Hiro immersed himself in research.

“I researched real oil tycoons and how they aged and what kinds of lifestyles they had,” Hiro said. “Those lifestyles affect how they age.” As Hiro did more and more research, however, he realized that there was no one look that defined the entire profession he was trying to represent. “Everybody looked so different, so in the end I relied more on the storyline and how this particular character behaved.” The idea, in keeping with the slightly heightened style of the film as a whole, was to exaggerate Cruise’s features but keep the character realistic.

Hiro began with a 3D scan and life cast of Cruise, which he used to sculpt his designs. His paramount concern was allowing the actor to be as expressive as possible under the makeup. “The important part is to make the prosthetic very soft so he can move,” Hiro said, noting that three weeks before shooting, Iñárritu called with a significant change. “He decided that Digger should be 65, not 76, so I quickly made a new design. Tom is around that age, but he looks much younger than a normal 65. Under his eye was exposed and the rest of the face was covered, but I made it thin to give him freedom.”

In addition to Digger’s face, Hiro was also tasked with creating an upper body for an early scene in which Cruise would be seen stripped down to his pajama pants. The body prosthetic was intended only for that one scene, with a lighter bodysuit created for the rest of the movie. “We made a light version of the padding for under the costume, because we don’t need to see the skin after that first scene,” Hiro said. “For the first scene we made a silicone prosthetic that was a lot heavier — the body padding was around 10 pounds, but the silicone was 40 or 50.”

During one of Cruise’s costume fittings, he told Hiro he wanted to feel the weight of the silicone throughout production. “He tried the body prosthetic on and said, ‘I like this, I want to wear it every day,'” Hiro said. “I told him it would be really heavy and hot, but he said he was training and would be fine.” Since gluing the body prosthetic on every day would be extremely time-consuming, Hiro created a strong spandex foundation and glued the prosthetic to it so Cruise could slip it on each day.

“He wore that for the whole film,” Hiro said. “One time he said, ‘This is so heavy, it’s really hard on my back.’ I thought, ‘Okay, you asked for it,’ but he went through with it and finished the film, so that was amazing.”

The legacy-quel is alive and well, and it only makes sense that a sequel/reboot/reimagining would eventually come for “Home Alone,” Chris Columbus’ 1990 holiday classic starring Macaulay Culkin.

There was buzz that Culkin over the summer pitched an idea to Disney as to where a grown Kevin McAllister would be today after enduring two child abandonments and harassment and attempted murder from bumbling bandits (our interpretation, not necessarily his read on Kevin’s childhood shenanigans and trauma). Disney now seems to have warmed to the idea like a cup of hot cocoa, especially thanks to the two additional names who are working with Culkin on the project: Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg. Disney’s 20th Century Studios is in early development on a sequel to “Home Alone” that would star Culkin reprising his original role and in which Rogen and Goldberg on behalf of their Point Grey banner would write and produce the film, working with Culkin on his idea, IndieWire has learned.

Things are very, very early days, and any plot details are being kept under wraps for now, and no director is attached at the moment.

#3573. Why Do AI Posters All Look Like That?

You know “the look” by now. Every poster for a business or event has pictures of uncanny-looking people, buildings that don’t look right, and always that one font. But why? If generative AI is supposedly able to “think” and be “creative,” why do so many of its results come out looking exactly the same? The answer is complicated, and it has to do with what chatbots define as “thinking.”

At this point, gone are the days of chatbots like ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini simply generating text immediately in response to a prompt. Some very fast models do, but most employ what’s known as “thinking models”, which are a bit of a misnomer. The “thinking” really just consists of generating a set of sub-prompts before executing the main one. And it’s in that hidden, generated text that most of the “choices” (to the extent that we can call the statistical output of an AI model a “choice”) occur that determine how a design looks.

To borrow a classic and implausible example, if you were to give an AI chatbot the instruction “Make a peanut butter and jelly sandwich,” it would start by generating step-by-step instructions on how to make the sandwich before trying to make one (if it could). Most of this happens invisibly in the background, and many proprietary chatbots won’t show you their in-process “thinking” prompts even if you ask.

In the case of an AI poster, it might break down “make a poster” into smaller steps such as “create a design brief for a poster.” To demonstrate this while doing some testing for this piece, I added additional prompts for ChatGPT to explain the “design briefs” it generated, which included details like layout, colors, and typography.

The problem is those instructions are still subject to the same flaws as any other AI-generated text. They can’t properly fact-check; they can’t walk into the real world and see the thing they’re describing; and they can hallucinate or fall back on stale formats that become easy to notice after a while.

For example, while testing, I had ChatGPT generate a poster for a Lifehacker-themed nightclub. In every case, the underlying brief it generated outlined some basic details, but occasionally it added things I hadn’t asked for. This included additional text, iconography, and in one case it even added the “design brief” explanation I had requested as the bottom half of the poster.

Those mistakes filter into the final product, when the brief is then fed into the image generator that ultimately makes the poster. In my case, ChatGPT showed me the underlying explanations for its reasoning (though even that could be different from what was actually sent to the image generator), but most people who use a chatbot for this task won’t see these factors before getting the final result.

While most chatbots won’t show you exactly what underlying “thinking” they use, most can be coaxed into describing the vague outlines of how they reached certain outcomes. And those descriptions provide some insight into why certain chatbots keep outputting similar results over and over. It doesn’t take long for some patterns to emerge. For example, any prompt to generate a poster for a nightclub almost invariably generated a brief that had specifications for a color palette including “electric purple,” “electric yellow,” and “electric pink.”

The reason for this should be pretty obvious: When the statistical model underlying LLMs needs to come up with an example for “colors for a nightclub poster,” the most obvious answers are neon, high-energy colors. Unless you know something about the specific club’s vibe (and write that out and feed it to the chatbot), the AI will have to fill in the gaps with something. And that something will be based on the same statistics it uses to predict any word.

This pattern of repetition was everywhere in all the design rationale ChatGPT gave me. Across multiple attempts to generate a Club Lifehacker poster, the generated design brief added an overarching “concept” that described the fictional club’s atmosphere as “high-energy” and “futuristic.” Every bot mentioned using images with the “silhouette” of either the DJ or a dancing crowd (often both). All the text had to be “bold” and “futuristic."

If there's one dead giveaway that a poster was made with AI, it's that one brush-stroke font that they all seem to use. Now, this is a bit more speculative, but I have a theory on where that specific design comes from. And it’s worth noting upfront that this seems to only apply to posters generated by ChatGPT specifically.

One of the most common factors I found in my design brief testing was the use of phrases like “brush lettering” or “brush script.” Brush lettering is a design term that refers to using any number of methods like markers, paint brushes, or brush pens to write text. In digital design, that can take the form of fonts that are designed to emulate the look of fancy, handwritten text.

In every test poster I created, however, ChatGPT seemed to take the phrase “brush lettering” rather literally. Every instance I encountered of a design brief that mentioned any kind of “brush” text generated an image with letters that looked as though they were created with a broad paint brush. A human designer would understand “brush lettering” to mean “something that looks handwritten," but ChatGPT didn’t seem capable of understanding the phrase as anything other than using an actual paint brush.

The generated posters aren’t even using a “font,” strictly speaking. (Often, letters that should be identical had slight variations.) The image generator part of the chatbot is still a diffusion model, so it can’t employ a vector-based font, per se. But the brush-style font is so common that its look surfaces in any statistical model.

This is an odd quirk of ChatGPT specifically, and it’s possible that it could change in the future. Especially if OpenAI intentionally tries to train this behavior out of its chatbot. However, it’s helpful to illustrate the underlying mechanism. The only way a chatbot can conceptualize design elements in a visual medium is to generate more specific text to feed to the image generator. And that text is just as prone to mistakes and blandness as any other AI model.

I’ve been examining this with a focus on the kinds of posters ChatGPT generates because they’re very common, but posters (or any AI-generated content) from other models might look different. Every model has its own tendencies. For example, a lot of vibecoded websites are made with Anthropic’s Claude, and you can often tell by the tiny text, buttons with rounded corners, and tile-based layouts.

To a certain extent, this is inevitable. While AI models are very different from humans and do not make “choices” in the same way people do, design elements still have to come from somewhere, and whether human or AI, it’s impossible to make these decisions in a vacuum. Humans will have preferences based on the things they like or emotionally resonate with, and AI models will have tendencies based on what their statistical model determines is the most appropriate output.

That means that an AI model’s “style” is naturally going to change over time. Even if a model improves or makes fewer mistakes, it’s impossible to ever change the fact that all ChatGPT images are made by ChatGPT. Whatever you generate with any particular model will have a lot in common with what everyone else who uses the same tool generates.

#3572. All 52 Deaths In The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping & Who Kills Each Character Explained

There are always going to be a massive number of deaths in any Hunger Games movie, as that is simply the nature of the franchise. However, the newest installment, The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, actually has significantly more deaths than the prior Hunger Games movies (except The Mockinjay - Part 2 when there is an all-out war, but those many deaths are largely not depicted on screen) because this Hunger Games is the Second Quarter Quell, in which 48 told tributes were reaped. Given that, there were always going to be, at minimum, 47 deaths in this Hunger Games.

Adding to that number, though, were two deaths that take place before the Games even begin and several that take place afterward, all having to do with punishing Haymich Abernathy for his rebellious behavior in the Games. However, unlike in the book, most of the tributes go unnamed and/or get very little screen time. By the first fight's conclusion in the arena, in fact, 20 are already dead. With so many deaths, many of which occur off screen and are never extrapolated upon, there are really just 12 key deaths that happen in the movie. Here's how each of those major characters die before the end of Sunrise on the Reaping.

Woodbine Chance is the first death in Sunrise on the Reaping, and he is actually why Haymitch ends up in the Hunger Games. Woodbine is the final name called during District 12's Reaping, but he decides to run off rather than be taken to the Capitol for the Games. As a result, he is immediately shot, leading his mother to run to him. In a devastating scene, Lenore Dove tries to interfere on the mother's behalf, and when Peacekeepers go to attack her, Haymitch steps in. Because of this, he is made Woodbine's replacement in the Hunger Games.

Louella, or Haymitch's "sweetheart," as she's also called, has a tragic death, despite her never entering the arena. Specifically, just as in the book, in the movie, Louella dies as a result of an accident during the chariot ride, wherein the horses become scarred from objects being tossed onto the track and ultimately run off, crashing into other chariots. In the book, Haymitch is described as being drenched in her blood, but the movie is not nearly as graphic. Still, her death leads to Haymitch doing his clap in front of President Snow—his first open sign of defiance that seals his fate.

The second District 12 tribute to die is Wyatt Callow, the boy whose family has made enemies in the district because they take bets on the Hunger Games. However, he eventually wins over his fellow District 12 tributes, and it's gutting that he dies, especially because it happens so early in the Games. In the book, Haymitch doesn't see this transpire, but he later learns that Wyatt died trying to protect Lou Lou. In the movie, audiences actually see Silka kill Wyatt as he runs to defend Lou Lou (who does get away, although her death soon follows).

It was always clear that Lou Lou was going to die in the arena, but the remaining District 12 tributes at least wanted to keep her as safe as they could and, ideally, prevent a death that was too painful. Ultimately, Lou Lou dies because she breathes in poisonous pollen from the plants in the arena. There is a slight change between how this is done in the movie and how this is done in the book, though. In the book, Lou Lou has a pump attached to her that sends drugs into her as the Capitol sees fit. Haymitch uses this to mercy kill her in the book. In the movie, he instead watches as she dies.

Ampert's death is absolutely devastating, especially because it's established that he was put in the arena (and marked for death) in order to punish his father, Beetee. Beetee even tells Haymitch earlier in the movie that he knows Ampert is doomed to die, and he simply asks that Haymitch not allow him to suffer. Unfortunately, try as Haymitch might, Ampert does suffer before his crushing death, as he's swarmed by ravenous squirrels who essentially eat him. In the book, he's described as being only a skeleton, whereas in the movie, he's gravely injured by the squirrels but he does not lose his skin.

Panache long seemed like the greatest threat in the arena, and he and Silka no doubt were, but Panache is taken down before multiple other characters. After an altercation between Haymitch and two other tributes, during which Haymitch actually takes them both out, Panache moves to kill Haymitch. Thankfully, Maysilee is nearby and uses poisoned darts to shoot Panache from afar, leading to his death. In the book, it's revealed that Maysilee actually fashioned the poisoned darts herself, using poisoned berries she found in the arena, although in the movie, that detail is left out.

Easily one of the saddest deaths in Sunrise on the Reaping is that of Maysilee Donner, who becomes a sister to Haymitch throughout their time in the arena. In the book, Maysilee's death comes about in large part due to her decision to kill Gamemakers who enter the arena during the Hunger Games. However, the movie doesn't show that scene, instead positioning her death as something that happens to punish Haymitch. In either case, though, Maysilee dies after a pack of vicious birds swarm, ultimately pecking her to death as Haymitch helplessly looks on.

In both the book and the movie, Wellie is one of the Newcomers, making her an ally to Haymitch Abernathy. In fact, in the book, Haymitch even actively hopes that she is going to be the victor after Maysilee dies. Sadly, that isn't ultimately Wellie's fate. Instead, she is killed by Silka as one of the final deaths in the arena. In the book, this is actually all the more horrifying, as Silka actually decapitates Wellie and then holds up her head. In the movie, Silka is still the one to kill Wellie, but she does so off-screen, using Wellie's bell to lure Haymitch to where they are.

Silka is one of the other ruthless, incredibly dangerous careers (although, notably, her story is one of the many changes in Sunrise on the Reaping, as she's actually shown crying in the book, but that was cut out of the movie), and she becomes the final person standing other than Haymitch. The two have one final fight, in which it seems like Silka is going to win—at least, it would, if audiences didn't already know that Haymitch is the victor—as she cuts a deep gash in Haymitch's stomach. However, when she throws her axe at Haymitch, he is able to use the force field to his advantage, sending the axe flying back at her, killing her.

Although Sunrise on the Reaping contains many heartbreaking deaths, there are perhaps few, if any, more gutting than the deaths of Ma and Sid because it is just outright cruelty, hatred, and proof that President Snow will do whatever he wants that lead to their deaths. Specifically, after surviving the arena, Haymitch finally makes his way home to District 12, only to discover his home engulfed in flames. He tries desperately to run to Sid and his Ma, but he's held back and informed that it's too late. In the end, Sid and Ma are buried in one casket, as they were found holding onto each other.

#3571. Steven Spielberg’s 13-Part Sci-Fi Series Is So Good, You’ll Finish It in One Weekend

Few things are as creepy as children in horror films and TV series. What's scarier? Children who are being manipulated by something — or someone — unknown, that is. It's doubtful that The Exorcist would have been as effective had Regan (Linda Blair) been an adult, or Sinister as seriously messed up as it is if Bughuul did his dirty work through senior citizens. This brings us to The Whispers, a forgotten, 13-part sci-fi horror series that premiered on ABC in 2015 from executive producer Steven Spielberg, where children communicate with an entity known only as Drill, who promises them rewards if they play his "games," resulting in a series of incidents that seemingly have no connection… until they do. Eleven years later, its creepy premise still makes an ordinary childhood friendship feel like a threat.

The Whispers opens with a playful scene, as children in a yard run through sprinklers, blow bubbles, and do what kids do. That is, except Harper (Abby Ryder Fortson), who's off to the side, talking to someone we can only assume is an imaginary friend she's named Drill. Her mother, Amanda (Autumn Reeser), calls her in, much to Harper's chagrin. She hasn't learned all the rules for the game Drill wants her to play yet.

What the game is, no one knows, but it involves Harper collecting tools and going up into the treehouse, where she's not supposed to be alone. Amanda storms out, but Harper won't come down, claiming that it's part of the game, and Drill says that Amanda is now "it." Amanda climbs up, walks to an "X" drawn on the floor, and promptly crashes through, hitting the ground, seriously injuring her and sending her into a coma.

It's the opening salvo in a battle against an unknown entity, one that may be supernatural or even alien in nature, and one that picks and chooses the children it "whispers" to further its own agenda. It's up to Special Agent Claire Bennigan (Lily Rabe), an FBI child specialist, and Wes Lawrence (Barry Sloane), a high-ranking Defense Department operative, to find out who or what Drill is, why he's targeting children for his games, and what his endgame could be.

It takes on an increased urgency for each of them, given they all have their own children. Additionally, Claire's husband, U.S. Air Force pilot Captain Sean Bennigan (Milo Ventimiglia), who was thought to have died in a plane crash, is part of Drill's game. And Drill's always one step ahead.

The Whispers seamlessly blends sci-fi and horror with an unsettling eeriness, deepening and building the mystery with an underlying, ever-increasing anxiety. (And yes, it's thanks to those creepy kids.) Each of the young actors in primary roles — Fortson, Kyle Harrison Breitkopf, Kylie Rogers, and Kayden Magnuson — is brilliant, playing innocents unaware (maybe) of the consequences of playing Drill's games (Magnuson is particularly chilling in the finale). The adult cast, too, is strong. Ventimiglia is the strongest of the adult cast, playing what is essentially two different characters in the first and second half of the season.

The Whispers also bears an undeniable mark of its executive producer: the exploration of the adult/child dynamic. The children listen to Drill and are willing to do his bidding because he listens to them, and the adults in their lives don't. From Hook to The Fabelmans to E.T.: The Extra-Terrestrial, there's a repeated theme of the disconnect between adults and children in Spielberg's works. Adults are absent, oblivious, and even antagonistic, and that's no different in The Whispers. The children are told that they're not allowed to talk to their imaginary friend. They leave their homes — despite so-called adult supervision — to carry out Drill's instructions in perilous ways.

While most Spielberg fare has adults learning to pay more attention to their children, The Whispers ends on a life lesson, faced with the consequences of adults not paying attention until it's too late. It begs the question: who is the real danger, Drill or the parents? It's actually Drill who makes the argument for the latter, saying: "If parents paid more attention to them, I wouldn't have been able to [corrupt them]. But they're always alone, watching TV, playing video games. So, who's really corrupting the children, Claire?"

But it's a question that would go unanswered, along with a host of others, with ABC pulling the plug on The Whispers after one season that ends on a major, unresolved cliffhanger. Don't let that stop you: The Whispers is the perfect weekend binge that keeps the viewer engaged from start to finish, and is a thrilling and eerie ride worth taking. Unless your child starts talking to an imaginary friend.

The Whispers is available to buy digitally on Amazon in the U.S.; a Prime subscription does not include it.

#3570. How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation

As soon as the first clips from DreamWorks’ latest animated film, “Forgotten Island,” started popping up online, there was one specific shot that caught on fire online — the lip pointing. It happens at a goodbye party for Raissa Molina (Liza Soberano), who is heading to Caltech. Her best friend Jo (H.E.R.) is late to the party and asks around to see where Raissa is, when an older woman points with her lips in the right direction. It’s a small moment, a visual gag that can easily go over the audience’s heads amidst all the other jokes in the sequence. But audiences familiar with Filipino culture immediately caught on to it, as did Latino fans and many others who recognize that gesture as the most potent and accurate way to point at something. Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

“That moment had been in the script since the first draft, because we wanted to put in as much as we can from our personal experience with Filipino culture,” director Joel Crawford told IndieWire. “Growing up around Filipinos, the lip point was something that was so specific and unique to me, so it’s beautiful that it transcends into other cultures. Adding that felt like a celebration of it, but also something that makes characters feel real. And in adding that specificity about the culture, it ends up being the most universal aspect of the movie because it invites everyone in.”

The lip pointing may not happen in a pivotal scene, or be important for a character, but it became a sort of symbol for the film’s approach to representation. Later in the film, Jo does the lip pointing because an animator thought it would be a good idea to reprise it, after learning about its place in the culture. Indeed, in addition to having an authentically Filipino cast and a cultural consultant to really capture Filipino culture, the animation team found their own ways of homaging or capturing aspects of Filipino culture to bring to the movie.

When creating the character of Jo, the animation team based a lot of her hand expressions on Filipino skater Margie Didal and her own hand gestures, while the villainous Manananggal’s movements were created by the animation team watching choreography done by Filipino-American dancer Phil Tayag, who brought a pop locking influence to the vampire-like creature.

“When we first approached DreamWorks and Universal with this story, it was important to everybody that we got every detail of this story and this culture right,” director Januel Mercado said. “

After challenging what was thought possible with DreamWorks animated films in “Puss in Boots: The Last Wish,” Crawford and Mercado push the studio’s visuals forward with “Forgotten Island.” With most of the story taking place on the island of Nakali, which is populated by all sorts of mythical creatures, to really capture the fantastical possibilities of this world, the movie’s visuals go wild, taking inspiration from 1990s Filipino art as well as anime from that time period.

For Crawford, the big lesson learned from “The Last Wish” was that you could take big swings in the animation style and the visuals, but you could also do specific things in the story with those visuals. Indeed, when it came to “Forgotten Island,” the idea of memories and friendship became not only central to the story of Jo and Raissa, but also to the eclectic visual styles represented in the movie.

“The idea became that we could push the animation styles to represent the different ways people recall memories,” Crawford explained. “We didn’t need to be limited by Western CG-style animation, but actually bring in some of our own nostalgia into it and make sure it fit the characters. When Raww tries to explain what happened when he met Jo and Raissa, he sees himself as way cooler than he is, so he sees himself as Goku or Guile from ‘Street Fighter,’ the animation going 2D in an action-heavy tone. But when we meet Mermahn, he is very shallow and narcissistic, and we felt his glamorous point of view fit the aesthetic of ‘Sailor Moon’ with the silly kind of heart-shaped lens flare.”

Still, just because you can go Super Saiyan doesn’t mean you let go of reality. Instead, the directors worked with the head of cinematography, Scott Cullen, to make sure the film had a live-action look to it. The idea was to capture the nostalgia of growing up, while being able to feel the camera in the space the action takes place in, as if it was a physical set.

“Joel and I really wanted to make sure you feel like live-action, you feel the cameras there, and the way the light interacts with the lens is reminiscent of tangible photos we grew up taking, where you don’t know how they’ll develop,” Mercado said. “ We wanted to add imperfections, and to have interaction of weather on the camera, like condensation of rain and droplets on the camera.”

This all added to making “Forgotten Island” look like a part of the evolution of DreamWorks Animation, while standing out as something entirely fresh and unique. As Crawford said, the studio doesn’t really have a specific house style like other big studios. “Every movie requires innovation and pushing boundaries and finding solutions,” he added.

#3569. 9 Calvin and Hobbes Comics from the 1990s that Prove Bill Watterson is a Genius

Watterson’s work with Calvin and Hobbes was incredibly versatile

Calvin and Hobbes creator Bill Watterson is a genius. Over the course of ten years spanning more than 3,000 comic strips, he developed two truly irresistible characters that are still beloved by millions. There was a lot behind the success of Calvin and Hobbes, but I think part of the reason why Watterson is still so widely respected is that he was an incredibly versatile artist who managed to do a lot of different things in an artform that can sometimes be limiting.

While this selection only scratches the surface of what made Calvin and Hobbes such a brilliant creation, here are nine comic strips from the 1990s that illustrate Watterson’s incredible range as an artist.

One of Watterson’s recurring themes in Calvin and Hobbes was his unabashed love and admiration for the natural world, a respect he channeled right into his two leading characters. Watterson returned to this subject many times and the points he made were always thoughtful. This one, from April 1992, is especially touching, as Calvin laments that humans have lost their “awe of nature.”

Sometimes, Watterson seemed to use Calvin and Hobbes as an outlet for whatever big, philosophical questions were on his mind at the time. In this comic strip, Calvin and Hobbes have an in-depth conversation​​​​​​​ on the nature of luck. The best part about it is that they have it in a little wagon, careening down a giant hill. Calvin lands in some pricker bushes, which he seems to think is pretty unlucky.

Calvin often spoke well above the intelligence of a 6-year-old, but these comics were balanced out by adventures where Calvin is just being an imaginative little kid, like in this Sunday strip from 1995 where Calvin imagines meeting an alien who camouflages himself as Calvin. The real Calvin then goes to school pretending to be the alien, which lands him in the principal’s office.

In addition to mastering the joke-a-day format demanded of comic strips, sometimes Watterson would tell longer stories which spanned several days or even a couple of weeks. For example, when his arch-nemesis, Rosalyn the babysitter, came over, their encounters often became epic sagas full of twists and turns​​​​​​​, like the story from 1990 in which Calvin drove Rosalyn nuts​​​​​​​ pretending to be Stupendous Man.

There were many Calvin and Hobbes strips which were incredibly heartfelt, like this tender comic from 1993 that merely shows a day in the life of Calvin and Hobbes, with both longing to be reunited​​​​​​​. The best part about it is its complete lack of dialogue.

While Watterson was capable of being thoughtful and heartfelt, some of his comic strips featured a surprisingly dark sense of humor. This side of him was best captured by the strips depicting Calvin’s snowman sculptures, which always showed snowmen going through horrific things.

This strip, from Jan. 21, 1991, contains​​​​​​​ three snowman sculptures in one. The first shows a snowman being shot with a cannon, the second a snowman being buried alive, and the third a snowman being hanged by a noose.​​​​​​​ That last one is especially hard to picture alongside more child-friendly newspaper comics like Peanuts and The Family Circus.

Like most other comic strips, Calvin and Hobbes had a simple drawing style, but occasionally Watterson would find an excuse to do something in much more detail, like when Calvin would pretend he was a Tyrannosaurus rex, like he does in this Halloween-themed strip from 1993.

For the most part, Watterson worked within the traditional bounds of newspaper comic strips, but he never let those traditional rectangles hold him back from a really creative idea. His dinosaur comics were a great example of this, as he liked to make his dinosaurs as big as possible. Another example of Watterson breaking the traditional format is this August 1995 strip, in which Calvin had​​​​​​​ an extended internal monologue about his parents being aliens.

Of course, a collection of perfect Calvin and Hobbes comics from the 1990s would not be complete without Watterson’s final comic, which ran on Dec. 31, 1995. This open-ended sendoff was beautifully understated and deeply poignant. It could not have been better.

#3568. The Out-of-Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: Looksmaxxing With Dangerous Drugs

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's column is bleak. First, there's the looksmaxxing trend where teenagers are taking dangerous chemicals to correct perceived physical shortcomings. Then there are the AI job interviewers. Depressing, but at least some young people are having a little fun with their dystopian hellscape.

You can judge a generation by the illegal drugs it pioneers. In the 1960s, hippies smoked weed and dropped acid to expand their consciousness; the yuppies of the go-go '80s fueled their drive to acquire with Colombian cocaine; but kids today don’t want to go deeper or work harder. They have a smaller, sadder goal: They take drugs to look better. The substance of choice for a growing number of teenage boys are steroids, peptides, and other exotic chemicals designed to enhance appearance.

Would-be muscle-men have been injecting themselves with black market ‘rhoids since the Eisenhower administration, but that was a small cult of adult weirdos with a specific goal. In 2026, kids are into it, and they aren’t using steroids to win a $500 prize in the Mr. Topeka contest; they’re using unapproved research chemicals to looksmaxx. Looksmaxxing is an online movement of young men trying to maximize their physical appearance. Teenagers are taking the normal desire to look their best to dangerous, pathological levels. Driven by a combination of undiagnosed body dysmorphia and relentless social media algorithms that turn amoral “red pill” kooks into gurus, teenage boys are ingesting a panoply of exotic and dangerous compounds in a quest to fix the angle of their jawlines, change their skin tone, lose weight, grow taller, and otherwise “correct” perceived physical problems.

In the "good old days" of steroid abuse, people generally stuck to abusing anabolic-androgenic steroids that had at least been tested for decades. Teens today are buying SARMs (Selective Androgen Receptor Modulators) and synthetic peptides marked "not for human consumption" from shady laboratories online. Steroids primarily affect the muscles, but many of these newer substances target different biological systems. A recent Rolling Stone article reports that kids are “heightmaxxing” by swallowing erdafitinib, a drug that treats advanced urothelial cancer, because the drug is known to trigger growth spurts (that can result in a curvature of the spine and other nasty side effects). They’re also trying MK-677 to get taller, an experimental growth hormone secretagogue that carries the risk of insulin resistance, water retention, and high blood pressure. Others are injecting Melanotan II, a synthetic peptide that forces a long-lasting deep tan, with side effects of extreme nausea and the sudden, aggressive darkening of moles. (And they're doing steroids too.)

In the looksmaxxing community, softmaxxing is doing generally-considered-acceptable things to look better, like getting enough sleep, exercising regularly, and eating a balanced diet. Hardmaxxing is taking more extreme measures like plastic surgery, smashing your face with a hammer, or taking experimental drugs.

In the bodybuilding and looksmaxxing community, “natty” refers to a natural, non-steroid-enhanced physique.

Here's something more lighthearted than the growing popularity of illicit self-esteem chemicals: the bicep heart and waist heart trends. The Bicep heart came first. Thirst trap videos started appearing on Instagram and TikTok in October in which dudes make a heart with their hand and bicep. Then people started posting variations where they frame the shot with someone they love inside the heart. The bicep heart quickly led to women posting the waist heart.

Okay. So maybe it's not that lighthearted of a trend. While there are some videos of dudes with skinny arms doing the bicep heart, it's mostly jacked dudes. And the waist heart doesn't seem like it would work at all unless you are a specific shape, as this video illustrates. So maybe this isn't a silly meme but an illustration of how young people are inundated with content that can trigger feelings of physical unworthiness, even if they're just looking for silly memes.

As if searching for a job wasn't alienating and horrible enough, some companies have begun using AI agents to conduct interviews. Begging a robot to let you work in a cubicle farm is as dystopian as anything Phillip K. Dick ever imagined, but don't count humanity out yet. Young people are sticking a finger in the eye of the machine by creating comedy videos that focus on trolling these AI job interviewers. They're hilarious because AI is the ultimate straight person in a comedy team, and the raw compute costs to run these interviews means corporate money is burning with each second of wasted time. Here are some of the top creators in the genre.

Bo Bongo: This YouTuber shows up to AI interviews shirtless but insists he's wearing a "corporate tube top," then focuses on daring the interviewer to notice he's doing things like smoking a cigarette or eating a rotisserie chicken.

Cam Whitt likes to wind up AI by arguing, interrupting, telling outrageous lies, and asking the dumbest questions imaginable, like, "When does the interview actually start?" and "How do I figure out what my name is?"

Grahamn Raabe: Among this YouTuber's schticks is speaking only in nonsense, like describing his professional background as "freight cadence, walnut, a little bit of Richard, spruce wood—six years of spruce wood."

Nick Reid: Is so obnoxious, he seems to make the AI furious at him, even though it's a computer without emotions. Two thumbs up!

#3567. Curry Barker Would Have Completely Reshot ‘Obsession’ If He Could

It’s been quite a year for Curry Barker. In September 2025, he brought his $700,000 horror film to the Toronto International Film Festival, where it sparked a bidding war that Focus Features won for $17 million. That hefty price tag turned into the deal of the century, as “Obsession” went on to become a half-billion-dollar box-office sensation, with audiences growing week to week. It was clear the then 26-year-old “YouTuber” (a moniker Barker rightfully dismisses) was something special. This was not just a flash in the pan, but a real talent with a seemingly boundless number of ideas and movies he wanted to make. His next film, “Anything but Ghosts,” was already in the can by the “Obsession” premiere, a yet-to-be-announced third film is in the works, while potential franchises (“Texas Chainsaw Massacre” and “Obsession,” Barker sees the One Wish Willow story device having “Knives Out” anthology-like potential) linger in the background. Related Stories Director Brian Duffield Had to Find a New Form of Visual Storytelling for ‘Whalefall’ How ‘Paper Tiger’ Evolved When Jeremy Strong and Anne Hathaway Couldn’t Reprise Their ‘Armageddon Time’ Roles

Which is why it’s interesting that Hollywood’s hottest new director took time out from editing (he’s cutting “Ghosts” himself) and writing (“I have my next thing that I’m working on — I’m really excited about it, and nobody knows anything about it, which is super exciting”), and an unexpected Oscar campaign (“Obsession” is a legit contender for Best Picture, Actress, and Original Screenplay nominations), to make a 5-minute short film, “Mama Bear.” On this week’s episode of the Filmmaker Toolkit Podcast, Barker talked about how the success of “Obsession” interrupted his established flow of churning out short-form content for his popular YouTube channel.

“I have two or three short films where I’m like, ‘Oh man, this all took off really quickly, and I have this short film idea I’ve been dying to do,” said Barker on Toolkit. “I actually have no time to do those short films, and then justifying if it be would be worth my time to do them when I need to be writing this, I need to be editing this, and I need to be doing press for this.”

It’s less about Barker’s desire to scratch the itch of the shorts he never got to make, but more about a hesitancy to step away completely from the iterative process by which he learned his craft — justifying the brief time he took off to make “Mama Bear” because he felt the need to sketch.

“It’s fun to have that playground because the features are bigger stakes,” said Barker. “We were like, ‘Okay, this is a short film: We can do weird stuff. Let’s come up with crazy rules that don’t make sense, and experiment.’”

Barker and his “Mama Bear” cinematographer — his young brother Riley, who worked on the “Obsession” camera department — created different rules for the camera, as Curry is still trying to hone his discipline for storytelling within longer takes. Not only would they shoot a narrow 4:3 aspect ratio, but the Barker brothers denied themselves the ability to move the camera left, right, up, down, or dolly in.

“I do have a lot to learn,” said Barker of making “Mama Bear.” “It’s so funny because I was having dinner and I told someone, ‘Oh, I’d love to shadow on Ari Aster’s set.’ And someone was like, ‘Well, you’re Curry Barker, what are you going to shadow for?’”

His 2026 meteoric rise has allowed Barker to collect a group of more experienced peers he views as mentors — including Aster, Bill Hader, Zach Cregger, and Rian Johnson — and successful producers, like Jason Blum, investing in his career, but he believes there’s a misconception of what comes along with “making it.”

“People think that once you’re in this club, you’re in the club, and everyone talks to everyone. But no — you’re in a bubble, and I want to know how Zach Cregger writes his outline. I want to watch him do it,” said Barker. “You’re all alone. Your process is your own, and you figure this stuff out on your own. Once you get into this league, there’s no one telling you, ‘Well, actually you do it like this, this, and this.’ It’s whatever you learned all along your journey; that’s your process.”

One of the most impressive things about the self-taught Barker’s journey is how quickly he turned himself into a successful actor/writer/director/editor. In 2018, when Barker left Alabama to come to Los Angeles to pursue a career in movies, he saw himself as an actor. Despite all the story scenarios dancing around his head, the idea that he would become a screenwriter was laughable.

“I never would’ve thought I was a screenwriter. I didn’t make great grades. I made Cs and Ds, and I wasn’t the best in English class,” said Barker, who naively assumed professional writers were the kids who won spelling bees: “I just thought to be respected as a writer you have to be that.” Barker credits taking screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s MasterClass as what opened his eyes. “It was the first time I thought, ‘I can do this, too.’ It’s really just about being creative and cracking a story, and there are rules, there’s structure.”

Directing organically grew out of Barker pulling together collaborators to shoot sketches and shorts for him to act in. Barker, half-joking, likes to say he realized one day that what he was doing was directing, and that he both enjoyed “telling people what to do” and had a knack for it.

What Barker accomplishes in a single shot — establishing a tonal balance that teeters between horror and comedy, combining blocking and camera movement to edit within the frame — is remarkably sophisticated. But Barker, who studies and strives for what masters like Kiyoshi Kurosawa can accomplish, quickly says he fell short in “Obsession.”

“Things that you might think we pulled off [with longer takes in ‘Obsession’], we reshot,” said Barker, who on the podcast described in detail a key early scene between Bear (Michael Johnston) and Nikki (Inde Navarrette) in the bedroom that had to be reshot because the action took too long to unfold. “I think Ari [Aster] said once that if you realize you needed to give this information in four seconds, but then it took 25 seconds, you’re stuck with 25 seconds.”

Curry Barker, the editor, is Curry Barker, the director’s harshest critic, giving him a bird’s-eye view of what he believes is the director’s inability to envision the required pacing of how a scene will play on screen, even if it might feel unnaturally fast on set.

“Every single oner that I’ve shot in my career has been a problem in the edit,” said Barker. “I think there’s two ways to fail at something. You can either fail, realize that it didn’t work, get scared of it, and then be like, ‘Well, in my last film I did a bunch of oners and then it killed me in the edit, so I’m not going to do that anymore.’ Or you can fail, realize how you did it wrong, and try to get better at that for the next time.”

As Barker discussed at the Future of Filmmaking Summit last month, that iterative process is key to how he got where he is, and it’s a mindset he clearly hasn’t given up. When asked how “Obsession” would have been different if he had more money, Barker doesn’t talk about locations, sets, special or visual effects, or scenes he envisioned that he couldn’t pull off — in terms of scale, he likes both writing and directing within set limitations.

“I would’ve reshot everything,” Barker answered without hesitation. “If I was finishing the edit before we got into TIFF, and you were like, ‘Dude, this is really good, we really love this movie, we think it has potential, but we want to give you $10 million to reshoot the whole thing, I would be like, ‘Deal.’ I would take it.”

“I think it’s so funny to look back and think about that now,” Barker catches himself, knowing he’s talking about a film that broke the box office and catapulted his career. “Now I wouldn’t change anything because I would be too scared to touch it.”

#3566. Avengers: Doomsday Star Reveals Major Power Upgrade For Returning MCU Hero

One of Avengers: Doomsday's heroes has been getting ready for his return off-screen.

Shang-Chi's debut expanded the MCU by introducing audiences to Ta Lo, a hidden dimension connected to his mother's family. The mystical location played a significant role in his origin story, as he confronted his father, Wenwu, and ultimately inherited the Ten Rings. However, his first solo movie ended without fully exploring what he could do with his new powers.

With Avengers: Doomsday approaching its theatrical release, new details have emerged about what the superhero may have been up to during his absence. Simu Liu, who first portrayed Shang-Chi in 2021's Shang-Chi and the Legend of the Ten Rings, has teased how the character could have developed and improved his abilities ahead of his highly anticipated comeback.

During an interview on the Countdown to Avengers: Doomsday Official Podcast, Liu joined hosts Iman Vellani, who plays Ms. Marvel, and Frank Alvarez to discuss his character. The actor also spoke about what has transpired with the hero between his 2021 solo film and the upcoming crossover movie.

Vellani theorized that he could have spent some time at Kamar-Taj with Wong, learning more about the origins of the Ten Rings. While Liu considered that option, he came up with his own idea that would reconnect the character with his family history. According to the actor, Shang-Chi probably returned to Ta Lo after the events of his first movie. The events that occurred during his initial visit to the mystical dimension left him very little time to explore his mother's home or develop relationships with the relatives who still live there.

Liu believes that revisiting Ta Lo could provide Shang-Chi with a chance to strengthen his connection to his mother's side of the family, like his aunt Ying Nan, portrayed by Michelle Yeoh. It could also allow him to learn more about the traditions and abilities associated with the realm itself.

Aside from the character's personal connections, Liu explained that Shang-Chi would likely be training so he could better control the Ten Rings. Although he defeated the Dweller-in-Darkness, the actor believes his victory did not necessarily mean he had mastered everything. He further elaborated, stating that Shang-Chi's victory was the beginning of his arc. Liu explained that he would have understood the need to practice and become more comfortable with his abilities before confronting the events of Avengers: Doomsday.

Avengers: Doomsday will be released in theaters on December 18, 2026.
