#3564. 10 Greatest Netflix Shows With Fewer Than 30 Episodes

Netflix has frequently proven that good things come in small packages when it comes to original television shows. Some of them had short episode counts on purpose, while others were canceled too soon. The number of episodes doesn't define a television show's quality, but it can play a role in how impactful the series is for audiences.

Netflix has released hundreds of shows over the years, and many were axed after the first season for reasons ranging from budget to low viewership. However, the streaming platform has a pattern of releasing critically acclaimed miniseries, and low-episode-count shows have been turning into cult classics. With that in mind, here is our list of the greatest Netflix shows with fewer than 30 episodes that are available to stream right now.

Once Netflix users watch five minutes of Blue Eye Samurai, they will wish they'd watched this show sooner. The show follows Mizu (Maya Erskine), a mixed-race Japanese warrior who is seeking vengeance against the men who may be responsible for her birth. She does all this disguised as a boy, and adjusts to being accompanied by Ringo (Masi Oka), and later teaming up with Taigen (Darren Barnet).

What makes one of the greatest samurai TV shows refreshing is the decision to redefine gender stereotypes, even though the characters don't know this is happening. Mizu's personal story is painful to take in, but it's her history that gives her the strength to fight and destroy the opponents who underestimate her. All the voice actors were phenomenal at turning up the hype, which will grow following the Season 2 premiere, and continue to build in the months leading up to the third and final season.

Although this show lasted only two seasons, Russian Doll has aged like fine wine thanks to the heart and unique humor put into it. The series follows Nadia Vulvokov (Natasha Lyonne), a software engineer who keeps dying and reliving her 36th birthday party in an ongoing time loop. The belief that she is hallucinating in a nightmare takes a shocking turn when she meets Alan Zaveri (Charlie Barnett), who, like her, is living in a time loop, and dying all the time.

Lyonne, who is one of the show's co-creators, is known for applying humor so naturally to any character she portrays, even in serious films or television shows. Her performance in Russian Doll was no different; and the combination of her personality with Nadia's made viewers see the connection the actress shares with Nadia, while watching her character learn about life and undergoing personal growth. Although Russian Doll may have become a show audiences have never heard of, they won't forget it once they watch one of its 15 episodes on Netflix.

Derry Girls was already one of the best dark comedy TV shows of all time, and aired on Channel 4 in the United Kingdom before it became available to stream internationally on Netflix. The show focuses on the lives of Erin Quinn (Saoirse-Monica Jackson), Orla McCool (Louisa Harland), Claire Devlin (Nicola Coughlan), Michelle Mallon (Jamie-Lee O'Donnell), and James Maguire (Dylan Llewellyn), in the 1990s during Ireland's political conflict, The Troubles. The teenagers go through typical, coming-of-age situations in school and with their parents, but as time goes on, they begin to pay closer attention to the political situation around them.

It may be hard to imagine that a dark comedy is also one of the most educational representations of The Troubles in the eyes of adolescents and adults. Every actor portrayed reality with grace, and it was phenomenal to see the show's plots backed up by archive footage of things like news stories, and a speech delivered by then-President Bill Clinton in Derry back in 1995. Although Derry Girls had enough popularity to last for years, series creator Lisa McGee always planned to end the show after Season 3, which makes it one of the best TV shows under 20 episodes.

This 10-episode miniseries is not only the greatest horror miniseries of all time, but it's also one that audiences may not want to watch alone in the dark. The Haunting of Hill House shows the terrifying story of the Crain family, and their experience living and eventually fleeing a haunted mansion in 1992, without the family matriarch. Years later, Stephen Crain (Michiel Huisman), Shirley Crain Harris (Elizabeth Reaser), Luke Crain (Oliver Jackson-Cohen), and Theodora "Theo" Crain (Kate Siegel) are estranged, but reunited following an increase of strange occurrences, including visions of their late sister, Eleanor "Nell" Crain Vance (Victoria Pedretti).

Every young and adult actor's performance is undeniably amazing, and their commitment to highlighting their characters’ trauma and coping mechanisms only makes the horror more real for viewers. Although the characters' experiences made this one of the scariest TV shows of all time, it also made viewers have a new appreciation for family members, especially their parents and siblings. Pedretti and Jackson-Cohen are among the multiple actors who returned to play different characters in the follow-up miniseries, The Haunting of Bly Manor, which is also considered one of the best horror miniseries.

Baby Reindeer is full of mind-blowing plot twists that fans love to keep up with. The show begins with Donny Dunn (Richard Gadd) attempting to file a police report after claiming he was being stalked by Martha Scott (Jessica Gunning), a lawyer who is no stranger to criminal mischief. Their encounters go from harmless to chilling, and her harassment worsens to the point where Donny is no longer the only victim in her latest round of stalking behavior. Although Martha's actions are hair-raising, they were needed for Donny to begin facing his fears, and accept who he is.

Gadd and Gunning's chemistry was undeniable in the most creepy way possible. The actors' passion in their performances proved to viewers that they were the only stars who could play these roles, and it was easy to feel Martha's anger and Donny's intimidation just by looking at their faces in all seven episodes. Their performances were only part of the reason why this show is one of the best miniseries of the 2020s, and they each took home a Golden Globe Award to prove it.

Mindhunter will always be a canceled crime show worth watching that deserves more than two seasons. Based on the true-crime book Mindhunter: Inside the FBI's Elite Serial Crime Unit, the show revolves around FBI agents, Holden Ford (Jonathan Groff) and Bill Tench (Holt McCallany), who, along with Wendy Carr (Anna Torv), interview and seek information from serial killers about their crimes and motivations, and apply that information to future cases. Set in the '70s and early '80s, viewers get an inside look into the early years of the Behavioral Science Unit, which is known for helping law enforcement with brutal crimes, and preventing terrorism.

Groff did not waste any time creating the personality of a no-nonsense agent seeking ways to improve the FBI. It was a 180 from his Glee character, Jesse St. James, and it showed viewers that Groff can go outside his comfort zone. The show could've had the potential to become an Emmy and Golden Globe Award winner if it hadn't been canceled, but it will always be one of the darkest TV dramas of the last 10 years.

Beth Harmon (Anya Taylor-Joy) portrays a chess player out for blood in this seven-episode miniseries. The Queen's Gambit explores Beth's journey to reach her dream of becoming a grandmaster, all while battling addiction and overcoming family drama in her birth and adoptive families. Her journey takes her all over the world with her adoptive mother, Alma Wheatley (Marielle Heller), and helps her form bonds with multiple chess players, including D.L. Townes (Jacob Fortune-Loyd), Harry Beltik (Harry Melling), and Benny Watts (Thomas Brodie-Sangster).

Taylor-Joy found the right balance between determination and intensity in her performance, and made it clear to viewers that she was the only person who could accurately portray the perfection-seeking Beth. Her character only wanted perfection, and when that didn't happen, a glimpse of the depression she hid from the world surfaced. Taylor-Joy showed audiences that even a perfect person is haunted by something, and her Golden Globe-winning performance helped make The Queen's Gambit one of the greatest Netflix miniseries of all time.

This German-language show is raw, complex, and one of the best sci-fi mystery shows of all time. Dark is set in Winden, a small town startled by the disappearance of two children, leaving families to suffer the collateral damage that comes of it. Jonas Kahnwad (Louis Hofmann), a teenager reeling over the loss of his father, soon discovers the disappearances, and other town secrets, are connected to a time-travel loop.

Unlike some sci-fi series, Dark puts characters front and center, and factors in their emotions when exploring the time traveling and supernatural aspects of the show. Audiences may still be surprised to learn it's one of the best Netflix shows with three seasons, especially since the complexity seems too much to fit into only 26 episodes. Everything came together by the end of the series, and while some viewers may now be afraid to start families, they were able to witness a satisfying ending that concluded all character arcs.

When They See Us is not only one of the saddest miniseries of all time, it's also based on the true story of the 1989 Central Park jogger case. The first two episodes center around the arrests of Kevin Richardson (Asante Blackk), Antron McCray (Caleel Harris), Yusef Salaam (Ethan Herisse), Raymond Santana (Marquis Rodriguez), and Korey Wise (Jharrel Jerome), for the assault and rape of Trisha Meili (Alexandra Templer), and the events leading up to their confessions and convictions. The final two episodes show the difficulty of some of these men returning to society, Wise's treatment in prison, and the truth behind what happened to Trisha in Central Park.

Every actor's facial expressions throughout the miniseries represented the pain the Exonerated Five and their families felt during the events leading up to their exoneration. However, Jerome's outstanding performance shook audiences to their core, and the Emmy Award-winning actor portrayed the fear Korey may have had in prison beautifully. The Central Park jogger case has become an example of racial profiling and discrimination in the media and legal system, and When They See Us provides viewers with a detailed explanation as to why.

Adolescence is a miniseries that's a 10/10 masterpiece that is both brilliant and terrifying. The four-episode show centers around Jamie Miller (Owen Cooper), a 13-year-old boy accused of brutally murdering a classmate. His arrest leads to shocking details about the events before and after the crime, as well as the pain his family endures from everyone who is furious at Jamie.

Miller's performance was unforgettably brilliant, and it's still hard to believe that this was his debut acting role, even a year after the miniseries premiered. It's usually difficult for an adult actor to give audiences chills for their antagonistic performance on a television show, but Miller had no problem doing so during the third and best Adolescence episode. Besides Miller, Stephen Graham and Erin Doherty were phenomenal in portraying the vulnerability and emotions behind each character, and their performances led to the trio each winning an Emmy and a Golden Globe Award.

#3563. How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. MUBI will release “Minotaur” in theaters on Friday, November 20.]

World-class Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev (“Leviathan”) returned to the Croisette this year in Cannes competition with “Minotaur,” having recovered from a near-fatal illness. After contracting a severe case of COVID in 2021, he reacted badly to the Sputnik vaccine and was put into a medically induced coma for 14 days. When he came out of it, his arms and legs were paralyzed due to Guillain-Barré Syndrome. He lay flat on his back for a year.

When he left the hospital in Germany in 2022, as he told me while at Cannes this year, he was in a wheelchair. While he says he hasn’t watched TV for 20 years now, “I watched a lot of films online,” he said through an interpreter on the roof of the Palais. “I read some things. I did not know if I would ever be able to walk again, to live again as a normal person. I have still now some consequences. I’m not at my best. I have regained completely the motion of my hands, but I have still a bit of a difficulty walking.” Related Stories How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation A ‘Home Alone’ Legacyquel with Macaulay Culkin in Early Development with Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg

But he did manage to shoot his sixth feature film last year, but not in Russia. After nine months of waiting, in the spring of 2023, he let go of one expensive project (“Jupiter”) for which he couldn’t seem to raise funding. “I said, ‘Let’s put it on ice, we’ll come back to it later. I don’t want to sit and wait for years and years for you to find the money. I want to make a film now.'”

So instead the filmmaker focused on a parallel project he had also been developing, an adaptation of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 thriller “The Unfaithful Wife,” starring Stéphane Audran as a well-heeled wife cheating on her husband, which was later remade as “Unfaithful” with Richard Gere and Diane Lane. The result, “Minotaur,” is the “Leviathan” Oscar nominee’s first film in nearly a decade, since 2017’s “Loveless.”

At the same time that the filmmaker was coping with his illness, four years ago, at the start of the Ukraine war, he made the decision to leave Russia and move to Paris. Going home would mean the risk of being considered a traitor or an enemy of the state in Russia. “It might result in us becoming what is called foreign agents; it’s a hard thing,” he said. “Maybe this will happen, maybe not. Let’s not be too pessimistic, but mostly all independent journalists are saying that their oppressions are going to get even harsher, and that I think we have decades ahead of us before things get better.”

His 16-year-old had been studying at a French high school in Moscow before the war. “His French was pretty good,” said Zvyagintsev. “So it was an obvious choice. And also, my wife [has been] in love with France for a long time, she has been learning French for many years. So it was a choice, also for both of them, and for their future.”

How’s his French? “Zero,” he said. “The other reason for me was that France is the homeland to cinema; that’s where cinema was born, and also there are so many cinephiles among spectators. Also here in France, directors have the final cut. In the states, it’s much harder to get in a position where you are not censored; it’s not a producer or someone who decides instead of you.”

The filmmaker set about creating believable Russian locations in Riga, Latvia, which still resembles its neighbor country. “The dormitory suburbs around Riga look exactly like Russian dormitory suburbs,” said Zvyagintsev. “A Russian eye would not be able to distinguish between Russia and Latvia in this instance. As for interiors, Anton’s flat was constructed as a set, so it’s a constructed set, and the villa where the main characters live is a contemporary building, a very modern one, and you could find something exactly like this anywhere.”

When it came to finding his cast, the casting director put out a call for Russian characters of a certain age. “Every actor from anywhere who is interested in working with you, they will send you a video presentation,” said Zvyagintsev. “They can be from Argentina, London, Moscow, Paris, wherever. You send them a scene they have to play, and they make a self-tape for you on their iPhone. Before, I despised self-tapes, but it’s convenient, because now with everybody scattered around the world, it’s the only way for us to work. We could not possibly pay for all the people I wanted to check to come to Riga to make a real-life casting. There were people also from Riga who do speak Russian.”

One serious issue for Russian actors still living in Russia was the possible repercussions of participating in a Zvyagintsev project. “I would talk to them about the script and show them parts of the script, so that they know what they’re getting involved in, because, of course, they were at risk of getting blacklisted,” he said. “Most of them, with heartache, refused to take part in the film, but there was one who accepted, and I’m still completely amazed at his courage. It’s the main part, the main character, [actor] Dmitriy Mazurov. I said to him, ‘Are you sure you want to film with me?’ And he said, ‘If I’m not doing this part, I don’t know what I’m doing in acting.'”

Of course, the filmmaker took a different approach to the Chabrol story. “In the first minute, the story is completely revealed,” he said. “We understand that she is being unfaithful, so then all the film is about observing him, observing her, trying to understand, hesitating, and trying to guess what is going on, and while he observes, the spectator starts doing it along with him. And after the murder, actually, he goes back to this position where he’s mostly observing her reaction to the disappearance of a lover, yeah, and she knows what’s going on, and again it’s about observation.”

The filmmaker loved one bravura sequence that is 20 minutes long without any dialogue at all. “The sequence after the murder, it’s 20 minutes, even a little bit more, with not one subtitle, so you only observe his actions, and there are no words: it’s extremely cinematic in its essence.”

And Zvyagintsev added many telling details from the real world, from corruption to the war. “The Chabrol film is much more classical,” he said. “It follows a pattern: he killed, then he’s discovered, and then he will be punished. And I wanted to break up this classical structure and to invent something different based on our Russian realities.”

Was shooting the movie a physical challenge? “When you are full of inspiration, when you are searching constantly for solutions, the light, the sets, the performance of the actors, you don’t feel fatigued in the same way,” he said. “There is such a joy in making the film that is, in your head, real. I think it’s the best drug there is.”

Next up, he will try and resuscitate “Jupiter.” ” I have met some producers who are interested in it,” he said, “so hopefully we will be able to get it moving again.”

#3561. ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch

Even six decades into his Hollywood career, Steven Spielberg is still synonymous with a brand of movie magic and spectacle that very few can rival. And when he decides to direct a new popcorn blockbuster like “Disclosure Day,” you know you’re in for a few dazzling sequences.

One of the most exciting moments in the film comes when a train collides into a car with stars Josh O’Connor and Emily Blunt close at hand. The sequence tested every department, from camera and production design to visual effects. And during IndieWire’s recent Craft Roundtables, VFX Supervisor Matthew Butler explained the unique challenge of incorporating subtle VFX work into a scene where so much happens in camera. Related Stories How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’ How a Filipino Facial Expression in ‘Forgotten Island’ Became a Universal Symbol of Representation

“With Steven, he wants everything to be as practical as it can be,” Butler said. “We had a real train. A real train, a real car attached to that train, it was being dragged on a real track. That actually did happen.”

But while Spielberg’s preferences were clear, Butler clarified that blockbusters on this scale rarely come down to a binary choice between practical effects and VFX. The biggest scenes often contain elements of both, as the pairing between in-camera human acting and cutting edge post-production is what leads to movie magic.

“When you combine some of the live action blue screen work, clearly that’s your lead actor and actress there, and your stunt work where it’s like ‘Oh my God, that looks really real’ and the stuff that you just can’t do that’s just too dangerous … that’s where visual effects came in,” he said. “But I wouldn’t say it was a visual effects sequence. It was a sequence that contained all of those, and it came together in the right way.”

More coverage from IndieWire’s Craft Roundtables will be published here over the coming weeks.

#3558. ’The Mummy’s’ Best Line Is Still the Greatest Quote in Franchise History

The Mummy movies are a celebrated blend of action, adventure, and comedy that still remain popular — and immensely quotable —decades after the first film’s 1999 release. There are many memorable lines that fans of the trilogy will quote to each other, from the swashbuckling Rick O’Connell (Brendan Fraser) declaring: “I only gamble with my life, never my money,” or Dr. Bey (Erick Avari) despairing: “When Rameses destroyed Syria, that was an accident. You are a catastrophe!” However, one quote from the original movie stands out as the greatest in the whole series. Spoken by Evelyn Carnahan (Rachel Weisz), it defines exactly why, with the fourth movie on the horizon, we hold the world of these films so close to our hearts.

For the uninitiated, 1999’s The Mummy follows Evelyn, a librarian and aspiring Egyptologist who, along with her brother Jonathan (John Hannah), free adventurer Rick O’Connell from prison so that he can help them find a mythical location, where they accidentally awaken the cursed high priest Imhotep. Along with a series of delightful action sequences, the film focuses on the clash of personalities between bookworm Evelyn and cavalier treasure hunter Rick.

It’s this difference in worldviews that leads to the film’s best line. In a drunken moment beside a campfire, Evelyn declares: “I may not be an explorer, or an adventurer, or a treasure-seeker, or a gunfighter, Mr. O’Connell, but I am proud of what I am.” Amused, Rick asks: “And what is that?”, before Evelyn looks to the middle distance, smiles, and replies: “I... am a librarian.” It’s a moment of comedy, but one that also sums up the charming relationship at the center of this film and the 2001 sequel, The Mummy Returns. Weisz was unavailable for the 2008 third movie, The Mummy: The Tomb of the Dragon Emperor, replaced by Maria Bello, but her return for the fourth film, currently in production, was celebrated by fans precisely because of the dynamic that this speech encapsulates.

The Mummy movies have broadly the same appeal as the Indiana Jones franchise, with exotic locations, ancient mysteries, and colorful characters populating a rich and entertaining world. While they may attract similar audiences, The Mummy differentiated itself from the classic Steven Spielberg franchise by making two characters the focus, rather than a single adventurer with a secondary character who serves as a potential love interest. The Mummy doesn’t work without Evelyn and Rick bantering, as well as using their very different skills in order to achieve their goals. Evelyn’s speech, while funny, highlights how crucial that dynamic is to the story.

Rick is strong, courageous, and charismatic, getting the group out of more than one dangerous moment over the course of the movies. However, it takes more than his heroism to get the job done. Evelyn’s brains, instincts, and curiosity are vital to their discovering hidden wonders, making her as important to the movie as her future husband. She is not a sidekick, or a damsel in distress, but an equal partner in an on-screen coupling that made Hollywood magic. There’s no Rick without Evelyn, giving her every right to cherish her love of knowledge.

The long-awaited sequel is set for a 2028 release.

The fourth movie in the franchise, The Mummy: Book of the Dead, is currently filming for a planned 2027 release. The first images of Weisz in costume as Evelyn recently emerged online, with fans delighted to see her stylish return to the beloved role. The popularity of the leak stems from fans who grew up with the movies acknowledging her as a vital part of the franchise, someone that audiences are keen to see as an older woman, a mother, still tearing across the world in search of adventure.

Many movies have had long-awaited sequels in recent years – Gladiator and Beetlejuice both got follow-ups in 2024, while fellow globe-trotter Indiana Jones came back for one last mission in 2023’s The Dial of Destiny. By the time the fourth Mummy film arrives, it will have been 17 years since the last time we saw an entry in the saga, and 26 since we saw Weisz play Evelyn. So why are fans so excited to see her back? Because, in all that time, her wit and fearlessness have been replayed on home video and streaming services for an entire generation. She is a character that endured because of her nerdiness, not in spite of it. We love this librarian and celebrate her return.

The Mummy has been adapted twice since this action-adventure trilogy was released: in 2017 as a Tom Cruise blockbuster, and in 2026 with Lee Cronin’s The Mummy. Both were poorly received, both critically and by theater audiences, and perhaps the reason for that is the affection with which Evelyn and Rick are held in the hearts of movie fans. Maybe you don’t need elevated scares or plane crash sequences to make a hit. Perhaps you just need a librarian.

#3557. Trump Renews Backing for Federal Film Tax Credit as Lawmakers Push for Year-End Passage

Looks like Hollywood could be heading into the new year with relief on a national level. The push to pass a federal film and television tax credit by the end of 2026 picked up momentum on Friday at a White House press conference, where President Trump said his administration was actively negotiating the measure and predicted it would pass.

“It’s running its way through Congress, and it has unbelievable support,” Trump said. He singled out Senator Adam Schiff, the California Democrat who introduced the bill with Republican Senator Tim Scott of South Carolina back in September, and said, “I tell you what, Adam Schiff said, ‘Wow, we love that bill.’ Adam Schiff said that.” Related Stories ‘Disclosure Day’ Did Its Biggest Stunts Practically, So the VFX Team Worked Hard to Look Invisible — Watch How World-Class Filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev Came Back to Life for ‘Minotaur’

Trump mentioned Georgia and New Jersey by name as states with good tax credits for film and TV production, but argued that those incentives alone would not bring enough production work back from overseas. With a federal credit, he said, “Hollywood would open again.”

Trump said his administration was also negotiating whether to extend the measure to benefit movie theaters, but said the matter was unsettled. He first publicly called for a federal production incentive in August after meeting with actor Jon Voight: one of three industry “special ambassadors” he appointed early last year.

The bill’s sponsors announced more than 60 new House cosponsors and four new Senate cosponsors on Thursday morning — with lawmakers from both parties signing on in both chambers. The following day, Trump himself brought up the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act in response to a question about whether he could work with Democrats. Calling the bill “very bipartisan,” he said, “I can tell you right now it’s going to happen.”

Trump gave no timetable, though earlier this week, Representative Linda Sánchez, one of the bill’s House sponsors from California, called for Congress to pass it before 2027 so productions could qualify for benefits on the first of the year.

“Members of both parties have watched jobs in their districts move overseas,” she said in a release from Schiff’s office sent to the press. “Momentum is on our side, and we need to strike while the iron is hot by passing this bill before the end of the year.”

A floor vote has yet to be announced, but multiple sources told IndieWire the measure would move faster if attached to a stopgap government funding bill. If passed and approved, the federal initiative would give qualifying film and TV productions a 20 percent credit on labor expenses for American workers. The credit could reach 30 percent for productions that qualify for bonuses.

For crews accustomed to watching projects follow tax breaks to Canada or the U.K., the proposal would give producers a clear financial incentive to keep that work here for them in the U.S. The bill’s new Senate cosponsors include Republicans Katie Britt of Alabama and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — as well as Democrats Chris Coons of Delaware and Dick Durbin of Illinois.

The AFL-CIO and the American Hotel & Lodging Association also endorsed the bill, joining a coalition that already included IATSE, SAG-AFTRA, the Directors Guild of America, and the Motion Picture Association.

“Given the support from Republicans and Democrats in both chambers and the president, we can get this legislation across the finish line,” Schiff said.

#3556. There's Actually a Simple Explanation for All These Widespread Outages

It feels like every time you look at your phone lately, another company is having an outage. Last week, there was Microsoft, whose outage took down services from Outlook to Teams. Then, the FAA grounded all flights across the U.S. following "communication issues." This week, a number of banks experienced outages, as did Apple. Even the NSA's internal communications network went dark. Some of the biggest corporations and organizations in the world can't seem to keep their services running, leading to widespread disruptions and confusion. When it's a one-off, it's an annoyance; when it's outage after outage, it starts to feel like a pattern.

That pattern, in turn, has begun to fuel anxiety among the general public. What could possibly be causing Apple, Microsoft, JP Morgan Chase, and the NSA alike to go dark at roughly the same time? Is it a coordinated cyberattack? An AI revolt? Is the end finally nigh? To an outside observer, it certainly appears like something coordinated and nefarious is happening here. Secretary of State Marco Rubio is insistent that there is "zero evidence" that hackers or bad actors caused any of these outages, and President Trump is particularly unconcerned by the whole ordeal, saying, "It's life," and "Things like that happen."

But to skeptics of the U.S. government, these trickles of information aren't necessarily reassuring. While I agree with calls for someone from the government (perhaps the president himself) to make an official announcement explaining the situation, the root cause does appear to be clear at this time: The short answer? AI is at fault here, but not in the way you think.

Love it or hate it, AI is a force to be reckoned with. While you might know that AI can generate hyper-realistic videos and manage your emails on your behalf, certain models are adept at discovering new security vulnerabilities in software. These models aren't just helpful tools; they far surpass the abilities of human researchers. You might remember Anthropic initially pulled the brakes on its breakthrough model, Claude Mythos, when it found that the model could root out security vulnerabilities in just about anything.

Mythos, and models like it, are a double-edged sword. On the one hand, they can be major assets for developers and researchers to find new security vulnerabilities that humans otherwise wouldn't have discovered, and patch them accordingly. Unfortunately, the same can be said for bad actors, who can use these models to learn about new security flaws and attempt to exploit them before researchers have a chance to find them. As such, software developers across the spectrum, from small-time devs to major corporations, have been racing to patch as many security vulnerabilities as they can find—and they're finding a lot.

You might notice your PC's security updates, for example, are shipping with more patches than usual—historic levels, even. Microsoft keeps breaking its own records with its Patch Tuesday updates, including over 1,400 fixes with its October update. The company's October 2025 Patch Tuesday update, by comparison, included fewer than 180 fixes.

It's important to understand that just about every company that develops software is furiously working to patch its systems before hackers or AI agents exploit vulnerabilities first. And while there are successes (Microsoft is now protecting its customers from thousands of flaws each month), this speed is also inadvertently breaking things along the way. That's not just speculation: According to The Washington Sun, both Wall Street executives and the NSA explained to members of Congress that patching security flaws discovered by AI models caused this week's widespread outages.

Barring some campaign to cover up a coordinated attack on systems and services, it does seem like these outages are simply the result of companies breaking their own products in an attempt to stop AI-assisted hackers from exploiting undiscovered flaws. But that's not all that reassuring, either. AI models are only going to keep getting better at finding vulnerabilities; likewise, AI agents are only improving at hacking into systems autonomously. Companies will need to ramp up their efforts to patch their software before both hackers and AI agents discover those flaws first, and so the cycle will continue. Unless something changes, we may see routine outages as companies try to fix things as quickly as possible.

The implications aren't specific to any one company, either. Our world increasingly relies on fewer companies to keep us all connected. We saw that last year, when cloud hosting providers like AWS and Cloudflare each experienced outages. When these services go down, so do all of the networks that rely on them. If AWS or Cloudflare break something while trying to patch their systems, whole parts of the internet go dark.

Of course, it'll only be more difficult for the general public—if not the developers themselves—to recognize when outages are the result of maintenance or a cyberattack. Just because recent outages don't appear to be nefarious in nature, that doesn't mean future outages will be so innocent. For the time being, however, it seems we can worry less about an active cybersecurity incident, and more about how AI is disrupting modern life in ways few of us saw coming.

#3553. It's Officially The End Of An Era For Marvel Shows

Marvel’s ventures have been very successful in 2026, but it is now officially the end of an era for the TV side of the franchise. Upcoming Marvel movies will move the MCU back into more mainstream territory, with two Avengers films, an X-Men story, and Black Panther 3 hitting theaters in the next few years. This comes after a period in which Marvel Studios has arguably put more focus into crafting small-screen stories set in the MCU on Disney+.

Despite a somewhat mixed bag of projects releasing between 2021 and 2025, Marvel’s 2026 TV shows have been excellent. Be it Daredevil: Born Again season 2, VisionQuest, and the brilliantly unique Wonder Man in live-action or animated ventures like X-Men ‘97, Marvel Television seems to be hitting its stride of late. However, in a cruel situation involving unfortunate timing, Marvel’s TV era is seemingly at an end.

2026’s VisionQuest was a huge success in many ways; from a self-contained story about humanity and grief to a sequel to WandaVision and a stepping stone to Avengers: Doomsday, VisionQuest worked on all fronts. That said, where the former and latter points are concerned, VisionQuest does seem like the end of Marvel’s TV dominance. The show is the final one before the release of Avengers: Doomsday, and the second-to-last live-action show confirmed to be released before Avengers: Secret Wars in December 2027.

What this means is that, besides Daredevil: Born Again season 3, which is as self-contained as MCU shows can get, VisionQuest ends the Disney+ era of the franchise before upcoming movies change everything. Avengers: Doomsday will begin the end of the Multiverse Saga and, with no projects but Daredevil: Born Again season 3 set for release in the main MCU universe between it and Avengers: Secret Wars, it will likely change the multiverse drastically. Adding in the soft reboot of Avengers: Secret Wars, which will change Marvel TV forever, VisionQuest is truly the end of an era.

VisionQuest ending the current MCU TV era only makes the future of the franchise on the small screen more unclear than ever. As alluded to, Daredevil: Born Again season 3 will release in 2027, though the show has been canceled beyond that, meaning it will likely end that section of the franchise. After 2027, only one MCU TV show remains in development: Zodiac. As of right now, it is unclear what Zodiac is, what it is about, or who will be part of the series. Moreover, it is set for release after Avengers: Secret Wars' reboot of the MCU.

Other than that, Marvel Television has only standalone animated TV projects to produce, from Marvel Zombies to Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man, which exist within their own continuities. All this reinforces how VisionQuest is the true end of an era for Marvel Television, as the future will only house standalone projects and those due to end soon, while the movie side of the franchise resets everything in massive ways.

Although the lack of clarity surrounding Marvel TV's future is worrying, VisionQuest concluded its most recent era in the best way possible. For one, on a broader level, VisionQuest was simply one of the studio's best Disney+ shows. Marvel TV has had as many hits as misses since 2021. The fact that the studio ended on such a high certainly makes things sweeter for Marvel and its audiences alike. Moreover, VisionQuest was a deeper, thematic conclusion for the WandaVision trilogy, which began in 2021 and has permeated Marvel TV since.

Not only was VisionQuest a good ending, quality-wise, but it signified the end of the Marvel TV storyline that started it all on Disney+ in 2021. Finally, VisionQuest's post-credit scene is one of the most exciting the MCU has produced in years, teasing Doctor Doom's upcoming rampage and the resurrection of the Scarlet Witch. This was the best way to signify the MCU's transition into the Avengers-fueled era that is about to ensue over the next year or so, only further solidifying VisionQuest as a fitting, exciting, thematically fruitful end of an era for Marvel Television.

#3552. ‘9-1-1’ Is Officially Switching Protagonists, but There’s a Big Problem

Editor's Note: The following contains spoilers for 9-1-1 Season 10, Episode 6.9-1-1 is just six episodes into its tenth season, but the show already just aired its mid-season finale. Any network procedural fan knows it's standard for each main character to get a couple solo storylines during a shorter half-season like this, except for the show's leads – which, since the beginning of 9-1-1, were Athena (Angela Bassett) and Bobby (Peter Krause). Since Bobby's death, Athena has been 9-1-1's main lead, while the other characters each get a significant storyline every few episodes. Buck (Oliver Stark), however, has been getting more storylines than everyone else this season.

9-1-1 continues to go in circles with Buck's character in Season 10, making him regress to the point of impulsively giving up the child he chose to foster instead of actually working through his trauma and self-worth issues. Five episodes have been dedicated to the Theo (Lincoln and Theodore Sykes) storyline this season, and every Buck and Eddie (Ryan Guzman) storyline this season has been about Theo. The latter wouldn't necessarily be a problem, except that 9-1-1 is still giving Buck way too much focus without real growth, while unfairly relegating Eddie to the supporting role.

After spending pretty much all of his non-work screen time this season supporting Buck, Eddie got to make a bold move in last week's episode when he chose to foster Theo. Even knowing that Buck would take this as a personal slight, Eddie prioritized the needs of Theo over the second most important relationship in his life – barring that with Christopher (Gavin McHugh), who cares deeply about Theo and even wrote Buck an angry letter for giving him up. 9-1-1 set up something compelling here, where viewers could see how Eddie adjusted to raising a second child, and how he's been feeling about this entire situation. This was the perfect opportunity to get a rare insight into Eddie's emotions, and to see the pain that Buck's cruel remarks caused him.

Instead, Eddie only gets a little bit of focus in the mid-season finale. 9-1-1 finally delivers the long-anticipated first scene between Eddie and Maddie (Jennifer Love Hewitt), but the whole scene sees Maddie treating Eddie coldly and accusing him of fostering Theo to teach Buck a lesson. Maddie hasn't been afraid to call Buck out in the past, like when he hurt Eddie's ankle in "Buck, Bothered and Bewildered." Here, though, she takes his side when Eddie isn't even acting against him, and everyone from the 118 except for Ravi (Anirudh Pisharody) also backs Buck up. Eddie doesn't get to talk about his feelings or his new role as a foster parent at all, and he instead oddly emphasizes the apparent importance of Buck's role as Theo's biological parent.

The Buck and Eddie pairing became so beloved by fans because of their deep friendship and care for each other. They always supported each other through the toughest moments and showed up for each other – until now. Eddie tried to give Buck helpful and honest advice earlier this season, but Buck just lashed out at him. Eddie later stepped up and did something really thoughtful to help both Buck and Theo, and Buck blew up at him again. Instead of having each other's backs like they promised they would before they even became friends, Eddie's been consistently monitoring Buck's back, while Buck can't so much as be bothered to turn around and look at him. Everyone this season is coddling Buck except for Eddie, but Eddie's still been exceptionally gentle with him, refusing to even accept his lackluster apology without also unfairly blaming himself.

Becoming a foster parent has the potential to be an amazing storyline for Eddie, but not in the way 9-1-1 is currently setting it up, where Eddie is just a stand-in parent for Theo until Buck is ready to take him back. 9-1-1 should focus on Eddie's journey of parenting a second child, as well as the memories that this will inevitably bring up for him from Christopher's childhood. Then, either Theo needs to stay with Eddie, or Buck and Eddie need to find a solution that works for them – because it would do Eddie a tremendous disservice to have him simply give Theo back to Buck after choosing to parent him. Considering the show has neglected Eddie's storyline all season, it's about time that he gets something more than just the crumbs of a storyline from Buck.

9-1-1 will return to ABC on Thursday, January 7 at 8:00 P.M. EST.

#3545. 10 Thriller Books That Hooked Me From the Opening Chapter

At any given moment, Scott Simone has at least three books jockeying for his attention. He’ll never turn down a campus novel with a literary bent, nor will he hesitate to add yet another mystery to his Leaning Tower of Pisa-inspired to-be-read pile — which is built upon the bedrocks of too many short story collections, how-are-these-real true crime books, and classics waiting to be cracked open again. Topics that have him ripping through pages the fastest include closed-circle murders, unhappy professors, life-questioning philosophical deep dives, so long as they feature sharp sentences, a dark sense of humor, and at least a little malice.

He’s spent so much time in book shops over the years he is, to his wife’s chagrin, continuing to build a library that doesn’t quite respect the dimensions of the apartment meant to contain it.

Some thriller writers seem terrified you'll put their book down, so they throw everything at you: a murder on page one and an abduction on page three, all while a massive conspiracy begins to unravel. And that’s all before introducing who’s involved. Eventful, sure, but there's something almost desperate about all that hoopla. It’s as if the writer's afraid one quiet page will send readers straight back to their phones.

The best thriller writers have a little more faith in their stories. They're in no great hurry to show their hand, allowing the reader to become acquainted with a character worth following. Of course, there's nothing wrong with opening on a murder or throwing somebody into immediate danger, but the excitement alone can only take a story so far. What matters is that the writer gives us time to find our footing, to become familiar with the world we're entering and curious about what lies beyond it. By the end of that first chapter, we might have little idea where the story is headed, but we're more than happy to go along for the ride.

A woman burning her father’s corpse in the garden is a shocking way to start a novel, but Liz Nugent somehow makes it relatable in the opening pages of Strange Sally Diamond. Sally's father constantly joked that she should put him out with the trash when he died, so she does. Yet the way she recounts it, with the practicality of someone listing yet another household chore, you understand it. It's an absurd explanation, but Nugent delivers it so matter-of-factly that you begin to appreciate Sally's reasoning.

That's what makes Nugent's introduction so effective: everyone else sees a 42-year-old woman who's done something appalling. The police have questions and turn Sally into a suspect. The neighbors are horrified and turn Sally into a monster. Sally is confused by all the hubbub. The reader is at an advantage here, having spent some time in Sally’s mind and following her peculiar train of thought, understanding her in a way nobody else does. The twists and the shock that follow only deepen that early compassion for a character that, on the surface, could be easily written off as psychotic.

When you’ve got revolvers and shotguns pointed at your head, it usually spells endgame. Lee Child flips that script when introducing Jack Reacher in the opening of Killing Floor. Reacher is simply eating breakfast as four police officers descend on a Georgia diner. But he doesn’t fly off into action, doesn’t protest or attempt to escape: he quietly finishes his eggs and tucks five dollars under his plate. Reacher, in fact, is so composed that the police, all that firepower be damned, begin to look like the nervous ones.

It's a clever way to introduce a man who'll eventually become one of fiction's most formidable tough guys. Child could have staged some spectacular show of force, but instead he lets Reacher's observations do the work: he sizes up the officers and considers their tactics. And just when we're getting comfortable with the idea that Reacher is an innocent man caught in an unfortunate situation, Child drops a revelation: he hasn't killed anybody in this town. He hasn’t killed anyone in some time now. It’s the exclamation point to the chapter, a way of announcing the police may have arrested the wrong man, but he’s not a harmless one.

Sébastien Japrisot begins A Trap for Cinderella in just about the most non-thriller way possible: lulling the reader into a fairy tale. Mi and Do grew up together. The former is the ideal of the pair: beautiful and wealthy, the symbol of adoration for everyone around her. The latter is intelligent but poor, always getting the short end of the stick. But then Japrisot reveals that Do has invented this little fairy tale herself. She resents Mi, so she’s conveniently cast herself as Cinderella. It’s presented in such a way that we’ve no idea how much of what we've read is true.

That quiet beginning is a trap in itself as the novel takes a dark turn, with a fire at a villa on the French Riviera. The blaze leaves one woman dead and another so badly burned that she loses her memory. The survivor doesn't know whether she's Mi or Do, and the fire may have been deliberate, meaning she could be either the victim of an attempted murder or the person who planned it. Japrisot has already shown how easily a story can be twisted by the person telling it, and then allows his protagonist to reconstruct her entire life from what other people tell her.

Jean-Patrick Manchette’s opening to Fatale is a bit of a red herring. Almost the entire first chapter follows a man named Roucart on a hunting trip. We become overly familiar with his protruding belly and his deep regret at giving up smoking. It's the sort of attention you'd expect a writer to give someone we'll be following for the next few hundred pages. So when an attractive young woman appears in the woods, we assume she's wandered into Roucart's story. But she takes a shotgun off her shoulder and shoots him dead.

Ultimately, it’s clever the way Manchette makes us almost as susceptible to this woman as Roucart. He was so enthralled by her appearance that he didn’t for a second recognize the danger. We, too, dismiss the danger, sliding past the fact that she just committed a cold-blooded murder because we're so intrigued by her composure, so curious about who she is. She arrives in a provincial town where the wealthy residents have plenty of dirty little secrets: they're a vain, greedy, thoroughly unpleasant lot, and watching her exploit their weaknesses becomes something of a pleasure. Before long, we're almost rooting for a woman we know is capable of murder.

Many a thriller makes revenge look easy, the only logical next step in the grieving process. It can look a lot different when you’re staring it square in the eye. That's the predicament Kōtarō Isaka gives a grieving father in the opening of Bullet Train. Yuichi Kimura boards a Japanese high-speed train intent on killing the teenager who pushed his six-year-old son off a rooftop. He's got the boy's seat number, a gun fitted with a silencer, and every reason to want him dead, but not the confidence. So when he sees his target, an innocent-looking schoolboy, he hesitates. The boy doesn't.

And that's how Isaka introduces one of the novel's central ideas: Having a perfectly good reason to do something doesn't mean you're remotely able to pull it off. It's bad enough that Kimura's been outsmarted by a teenager, but worse, the boy finds his humiliation entertaining. And Isaka has plenty more fun at the expense of his characters as the train fills with professional killers, all convinced they know what they're doing. They're a dangerous bunch, sure, but for all their cleverness and carefully laid plans, they spend an awful lot of time making fools of themselves.

Jo Nesbø warps a symbol of winter wonderland into one of holiday horror in the opening pages of The Snowman. Sara Kvinesland meets her lover at his house, leaving her young son waiting in the car. She's nervous about someone catching them, so when her lover notices a face staring at them through the bedroom window, they both panic. But it's only a snowman, its pebble eyes fixed on the house. Except, snowmen don't build themselves — somebody went to the trouble of putting it right outside that window.

Nesbø lets that thought linger as Sara returns to her car, where her son is trembling behind locked doors, seeing something that's scared him half to death. Sara's got other things on her mind: she's worried about her affair and keeping up appearances. Her son can barely get her attention, even when he tells her they're going to die. And that's where Nesbø really gets under your skin: the boy knows something's wrong, but Sara, the one person who really should be listening, is too distracted to notice. There's no murder and no grisly discovery; just a snowman standing outside a house, and already we’re hooked.

Thirteen Hours opens at 5:36 a.m. with a woman running for her life. We don’t know why, or who’s chasing her, and we don’t find out. Deon Meyer leaves her, exhausted and terrified, desperate to escape the men who seem to want her dead. Meyer cuts to Detective Benny Griessel, who's being dragged out of bed by a phone call about a body outside a church. And the man’s got problems of his own: an estranged wife, another woman he slept with recently, and a 156-day desperate attempt to stay sober.

It's almost infuriating how casually Meyer abandons the woman, but that frustration only makes us more desperate to get back to her. Griessel, of course, hasn't the faintest idea she exists, and Meyer takes his time introducing the detective, giving us a man whose considerable professional experience is at odds with the mess he's made of his personal life. Each time Meyer takes us away from the woman, we're left worrying about what's happening to her while we're gone. And all the while, the clock keeps ticking, whether we're watching the woman running or not.

An ex-con in a stolen car isn't exactly the person you'd entrust with an 11-year-old girl's safety, but Jordan Harper has us begging her to climb inside in the opening of She Rides Shotgun. You see, a prison gang has ordered the murder of Nate McClusky and his family, and he's racing to get his daughter Polly before the killers do. But Polly doesn't know: all she sees outside her school is a hulking man covered in tattoos and scars, a father she barely remembers and who's supposed to be behind bars.

Harper puts us in an uncomfortable position, knowing that the man Polly fears might be the only person capable of protecting her. And he plays with that contradiction throughout their uneasy reunion. Polly is painfully shy and bullied at school, carrying a teddy bear for comfort. Nate looks like he could frighten just about anybody. But as they're driving away, a police car passes, and Polly catches something on her father's face she'd never expected to see: fear. Now this intimidating man doesn't seem so invincible, and that's what makes the opening so compelling.

It's a familiar enough scene: a mother worried about a son who's out past his curfew. But Gillian McAllister takes that moment of parental anxiety to the extreme in the opening of Wrong Place Wrong Time. Jen is waiting up for her 18-year-old son, Todd, watching from the window of their Liverpool home as he finally comes down the street. She's relieved to see him, until a stranger approaches. Todd pulls a knife and stabs the man three times, and she hasn't the faintest idea why.

It's a horrible thing for a parent to witness, made worse by the realization that the child you've spent 18 years raising might be someone you don't know at all. McAllister gives Jen a chance to go back and find out. We watch as the clocks move backward through the rest of the novel, allowing her to revisit the days leading up to the murder. She knows who wielded the knife but not what drove him to it. This literal trip down memory lane allows her to scrutinize the years she's spent raising him, revisiting conversations and decisions she'd long since forgotten.

It's easy to imagine what you'd do if someone broke into your house: grab the children, call the police, find something to defend yourself with. But Tracy Sierra makes those plans laughably optimistic in the opening of Nightwatching, in which a mother hears footsteps on the stairs. She entertains just about every possibility until a stranger appears at the top of the stairs, so tall he nearly hits his head on the ceiling. Even then, she struggles to accept what's happening.

Sierra makes us endure every second of that hesitation, making the mental cycle of decisions seem visceral. She thinks of screaming, but doesn’t want the intruder to know she’s there. She thinks about moving, but doesn’t want to wake the children. All the while, her mind also keeps latching onto the most random of details, from the man's dry sneakers to the light falling across the landing. There's something convincing about the way she thinks, grasping at anything that might help her understand the situation while struggling to do something about it.

The Paramount+ hit thriller finally delivers on the survivors’ harrowing return home across its gripping first eight episodes

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For five years and three seasons, Paramount’s “Yellowjackets” has been at once enthralling and appalling audiences. As someone who is easily squeamish, I’ll admit that when I first tuned in years ago, I almost abandoned the show altogether, too disturbed by watching teenagers hunt their friends like animals and decapitate corpses to continue.

What eventually roped me in and made it impossible to look away were the stellar performances from the massive ensemble cast and the storytelling that — cliché as it sounds — actually left me on the edge of my seat, peeking out in horror from behind my fingers. Adding to that was “Yellowjackets’” knack for unveiling mysteries that left viewers, myself included, desperate for answers.

Heading into the show’s fourth and final season, though, those strengths become double-edged swords. The major questions that kept audiences hooked for years now demand answers before the series finale. Likewise, the interwoven narrative — jumping between the teenage plane crash survivors stranded in the wilderness and their adult counterparts — has always been an effective tool, but before the end, these timelines need to find a satisfying cohesion.

Having watched the first eight of season 4's 10 episodes, I can safely and somewhat unfortunately say that while “Yellowjackets” satisfies in some areas, it falls short in others — and it doesn’t have much time left to course-correct.

Easily the most compelling aspect of these first eight episodes is the exploration of the team’s return home. For three seasons, audiences knew these traumatized kids — the ones who survived, at least — would eventually make it back, with the adult timeline confirming several names (Shauna, Misty, and Melissa among them).

Prior to season 4, however, “Yellowjackets” had yet to reveal that exact moment of return and its immediate fallout: watching characters who hunted, killed, and ate their friends attempt to slip back into their “normal” lives. While the adult timeline already proved the survivors never truly moved past their ordeal, seeing their parent reunions, the jarring shift in high school social dynamics, and the strange fame that comes with surviving a mass tragedy is precisely what audiences have been waiting for.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

With just two episodes to go, a shocking number of questions remain on the table, raising an obvious concern: has “Yellowjackets” saved too much for an epic finale? Of the many shows met with controversy over their endings, the mind-bending sci-fi series “Lost” is among the most notorious and perhaps the closest comparison to “Yellowjackets” in its approach to mystery and suspense.

Like “Lost,” “Yellowjackets” has spent years building complex mysteries whose reveals appear to be crammed into the final two episodes. In the case of “Lost,” that famously backfired, leaving even dedicated fans frustrated by how questions were answered, the breakneck speed with which some were “resolved,” or the fact that certain mysteries went unaddressed forever.

Based on episodes 1 through 8, “Yellowjackets” season 4 seems to be heading down a very similar path. Several of the show’s most captivating questions haven't just gone unanswered by the end of episode 8, they’ve been largely ignored. Hopefully, this doesn't mean answers are never coming, which would undoubtedly trigger a wave of backlash akin to “Lost.” Even if the finale delivers, it would have been far more satisfying to see this final season deeply flesh out the truth of the wilderness — whether it’s a supernatural force or simply a manifestation of the survivors’ trauma — well before the final curtain.

Ultimately, “Yellowjackets” Season 4 is an exciting final entry that showcases the cast at the top of their game and finally gives audiences a real look at how the survivors reacclimated—or failed to—after nearly two years in the wild. Still, for the final chapter of a show that has captivated viewers for five years, the series has left itself too much ground to cover in too little time.

While heavy narrative exposition was always inevitable in Season 4—especially with so much left unresolved in the adult timeline—what audiences really want heading into the finale are answers, not more questions. With the clock very much ticking, “Yellowjackets” still has to prove it can stick the landing.

You might not be able to run Siri AI, but these iOS 27 upgrades are genuinely worth installing

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Most of the conversation around iOS 27 was centered on Apple’s upgraded, AI-powered Siri, which brings deeper on-screen awareness and smarter multi-step actions. The catch is that Apple Intelligence requires an iPhone 15 Pro or newer, leaving anyone holding onto an older compatible handset locked out of the headline feature.

If you have been putting off the update assuming there is nothing in it for older hardware, it is worth reconsidering. Beneath the AI marketing, Apple rolled out several high-impact security, camera, and interface upgrades that run without Apple Intelligence — and these three additions make a meaningful difference in daily use.

Scammers frequently rely on high-pressure calls and spoofed texts to trick you into wiring funds or surrendering credentials. Introduced in iOS 27, Impersonation Risk Detection serves as Apple’s built-in defense against this social engineering, and it works without requiring Apple Intelligence.

The system monitors on-device interaction patterns and behavioral cues during high-stakes actions without reading your personal messages, emails, or photos. If you attempt a large transfer or sensitive account change under signs of coercion, your iPhone flags the event and directs supported banking apps to require secondary verification before funds can leave your account.

Over the last few iOS updates, Apple has tucked more manual toggles behind the Camera app’s six-dot menu, adding extra taps whenever you want to tweak exposure, aspect ratio, or timer settings before taking a shot. iOS 27 fixes that friction by letting you pin your essential controls directly to the top of the viewfinder.

Launch the Camera app, tap the six-dot icon and hit Edit in the top-left corner. From there, tap any highlighted tools you want kept within thumb’s reach, remove shortcuts you rarely touch using the minus badge, and tap Done.

Even better, iOS 27 saves separate pinned layouts per shooting mode, allowing you to tailor your quick-access toolbar individually for Photo, Portrait, Video, Cinematic, Slow-Mo, and Time-Lapse.

Apple’s translucent Liquid Glass design has remained one of iOS’s most polarizing visual shifts since its debut, particularly when semi-transparent menus sit over bright or busy wallpapers. Rather than forcing a one-size-fits-all look, iOS 27 introduces a dedicated precision slider so you can tailor how much transparency appears across your system interface.

Open Settings, tap Appearance, and select Liquid Glass to find the new control. Sliding the toggle to the left preserves the full see-through glass aesthetic, while moving it to the right applies a heavier, tinted backdrop that makes buttons and text significantly easier to read at a glance.

A live preview window sits directly above the slider so you can test the contrast before locking in your preferred look.

#3536. HBO Max's 4-Part Sci-Fi Epic Is One of the Best on Any Streaming Platform

Most science fiction franchises tend to try to reinvent themselves over the years, with mixed results. Some, like Star Wars, return with new installments that often spark divisive discourse. Others, like Blade Runner or Tron, have extremely lengthy gaps between sequels. One sci-fi franchise not only reinvented itself in the early 2010s but also delivered a truly epic scale that very few blockbusters have matched. This honor goes to the Planet of the Apes reboot series, which is available to stream on Hulu and Prime Video.

Starting with Rise of the Planet of the Apes, the new films focus on the birth of the titular Planet of the Apes, especially how the apes evolve into the dominant species on the planet. It's not the first time someone has tried to reboot the series; Tim Burton launched his own version of Planet of the Apes in 2001, and James Cameron was even approached to revive the series on film before he eventually made Titanic. The new Planet of the Apes succeeds because it takes the time to show how its world is constantly evolving, offering a sense of growth that other sci-fi franchises lack. It also doesn't hurt that one of Hollywood's best directors helped take the series to a new level.

In the original Planet of the Apes, humanity has devolved into a mute class of workers while the apes lord over them. This led to arguably one of the greatest twists in science fiction history, in which George Taylor (Charlton Heston) discovers that the "planet" he's landed on is actually Earth, ravaged by nuclear war. Rise of the Planet of the Apes shifts from a nuclear threat to a viral one, as scientist Will Rodman (James Franco) creates a drug called ALZ-112 to reverse the effects of Alzheimer's disease.

While ALZ-112 increases the intelligence of the chimpanzee Caesar (Andy Serkis), it proves to be deadly to humans, triggering a global pandemic. Director Rupert Wyatt also said that future films would explore the conflict between man and ape:

"We've incorporated elements from Conquest of the Planet of the Apes, in terms of how the apes begin to revolt, but this is primarily a prequel to the 1968 film... Caesar is a revolutionary figure who will be talked about by his fellow apes for centuries... This is just the first step in the evolution of the apes, and there's a lot more stories to tell after this. I imagine the next film will be about the all-out war between the apes and humans."

True to Wyatt's words, the next two films, Dawn of the Planet of the Apes and War for the Planet of the Apes, focused on how humanity and apes came to battle. It also brought a new director into the fold, as Matt Reeves stepped up to helm both sequels. Reeves brought a truly epic scale to the Planet of the Apes reboot, showcasing just how much the world changed in the wake of humanity's decimation. Rain-soaked forests, snow-covered terrain, and a massive military fortress are given plenty of sweeping shots, with cinematographer Michael Seresin taking time to close in on both human and apes' facial expressions — letting their eyes say much more than words could. Reeves' vision led to critical and commercial success for both Apes sequels, and paved the way for his work on The Batman.

A good score elevates a film's emotional impact. A great score affects you long after the movie's over. Here are a few examples of that excellence.

There's one person who helped make the Planet of the Apes reboot a bona fide success, and it's Andy Serkis. Serkis delivers a career-best performance as Caesar, thanks to a blend of motion capture and a truly magnetic performance. Every time Caesar is on-screen, the camera gravitates toward him, showcasing his transformation from a mere ape to a leader to a messianic figure. Even in death, Caesar continues to cast a large shadow as Kingdom of the Planet of the Apes shows how apes have taken up his words, for good and ill. It's also led the Planet of the Apes reboot to continue topping the streaming charts, showing that the new films have just as strong a hold on modern audiences as the original Planet of the Apes did on its audience.

The Planet of the Apes reboot proves that not every reboot of a popular franchise needs to rely on nostalgia or simply rehash the original story. It also showcases that there's still room for sweeping epics in the sci-fi landscape, especially as Dune: Part Three gears up to hit theaters.

People obtained Kimmarie's death certificate ... and the outlet reports that cardiopulmonary arrest is listed as her primary cause of death.

As temperatures drop, our lawns often show signs of wear and tear from battling the elements. Whether dealing with patchy growth, damaged areas, or waterlogged soil, we still need to give our yards extra lawn care for the harsh winter months ahead.

Perhaps one of the most important gardening tasks for healthy lawn growth is applying fertilizer. However, given the cooler conditions, is it too late to fertilize my lawn before winter?

To answer my question, I called on the gardening experts to answer this question — and offer their top tips and tricks. So before you prep your lawn fertilizer, here’s what you need to know.

According to experts, you can fertilize your lawn before winter — as long as it’s completed by mid-November at the latest.

“If you are looking to fertilize your lawn before winter, I would recommend you do this no later than the middle of November, as your grass is becoming dormant and growth is slowing around this time, so it is best to fertilize beforehand,” advises Craig Wilson, co-founder and gardening expert at Gardeners Dream.

While fertilizing is commonly associated with warmer weather, cold-weather lawn care relies on specialized formulas.

“Make sure to use a low-nitrogen fertiliser that features high-potassium levels, as this will help to protect your lawn better in the cold weather,” adds Wilson.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Fall fertilization supports stronger root systems, thicker turf, and lends better resistance to harsh conditions throughout the winter months.

Furthermore, choose a fertilizer designed to specifically help your lawn withstand and handle colder weather conditions.

“Fall fertilization supports stronger root systems, thicker turf, and lends better resistance to harsh conditions throughout the winter months,” states Brian Feldman, Senior Director of Operations and Agronomy at TruGreen.

“Make sure to select a fertilizer that’s formulated specifically for fall and apply it about 3-4 weeks before your area’s first expected frost, and while soil temperatures are still above 50 degrees F.”

Of course, prepping your lawn for winter requires a few extra steps, including clearing away weeds, clearing fallen leaves, and debris to stop them from smothering the soil underneath.

“I would also advise continuing to keep your lawn clear of fallen leaves to avoid any dead patches of grass,” agrees Wilson.

“They needn’t go to waste though — you can spread them over your borders as a nutritious mulch for your plants, which will help improve the soil quality!”

While adding excess fertilizer seems like a good way to protect your lawn through the winter, it can actually do more harm than good. Avoid over-fertilizing if you don’t want to damage your lawn.

“Be careful not to over-fertilize, as too much can lead to nutrient runoff and weak, fast-growing grass that’s more prone to damage. The goal is strong, sustained growth from the roots up,” adds Feldman.

Other top tips include aerating your lawn and knowing when to plant grass seed in November.

The science fiction genre has always prided itself on bringing stories that seem impossible to adapt to life. Although the genre has thrived for myriad reasons, one of the most important aspects is how wellsci-fi shows build their worlds. Several series have made this seem easy, when it is anything but. The Expanse, Battlestar Galactica, Foundation, and other sci-fi franchises have remained so influential in the space because they understand that a series with a world that doesn’t work won't grip audiences for long.

Prime Video could soon have another ambitious space opera on its hands that has the potential to surpass the likes of sci-fi giants like The Expanse and Battlestar Galactica. However, it has to get several elements of its source material right to achieve that admirable feat. In late 2024, Prime Video announced they would adapt James S.A. Corey’s expansive novel series, The Captive’s War, into a TV show.

For fans of The Expanse, this news was welcome, but it also brought the genre-typical fear that the source material would be poorly adapted. However, The Captive's War could be Prime Video’s next flagship sci-fi series because it could give the streaming platform a chance to explore a different side of the genre. The source material for The Captive’s War series indicates that it is simply not going to be another version of The Expanse, but a TV show with an entirely new universe.

Prime Video’s adaptation of The Captive’s War could completely change how sci-fi is brought to life on streaming platforms. Following humanity after the alien Carryx empire invades the planet Anjiin and abducts a group of humans, The Captive’s War presents a staggering world.

The first book in the series, The Mercy of Gods, is a slow burn and takes a while to get going, but once it does, the story takes on a life of its own. Corey’s novels feature a variety of alien planets, rich biology, and strange aliens, particularly the Carryx. The novels’ extensive world creates a strong foundation for worldbuilding because some of these aliens are so fascinating. The Carryx, in particular, represents an entire civilization, social structures, and history that make Corey’s story even more interesting.

With the amount of information in the source material, it's kind of difficult to imagine how it will all come together. Even The Captive's War ​​​​​​authors Daniel Abraham and Ty Franck have acknowledged that the books feature spectacular alien species and complicated internal character perspectives that will make the television adaptation challenging. However, there is some hope. Prime Video’s adaptation of The Captive’s War is stacked with an incredible creative team.

Naren Shankar, who served as showrunner on The Expanse, and director Breck Eisner, who also worked on the space opera, will helm the adaptation of The Captive’s War. Shankar is attached as writer and showrunner, Eisner as director, while Abraham and Franck are also involved in writing the adaptation. They've already proven their mettle with The Expanse, so this creative dream team should help to quell book fans' fears about the adaptation.

Given that The Captive’s War and The Expanse were written by the same author, comparisons between the novels are inevitable. Though both stories demonstrate a perfect understanding of science fiction worldbuilding, they approach the concept from very different perspectives. Corey's hard sci-fi novel focuses primarily on humanity's expansion across the solar system, whereas The Captive's War imagines an enormous galactic civilization.

Political worldbuilding is the main reason The Expanse became so compelling, particularly through its exploration of the competing interests of Earth, Mars, and the Belt. Arguably, The Captive's War’s political maneuvering is even more interesting, especially because the story explores an alien civilization built around conquest, domination, and the exploitation of other species.

What science fiction novels resonate the most with Goodreads users? The top-rated books in the genre and how many times they've been rated tell us.

All in all, The Captive's War’s setting is much larger than The Expanse and has more diverse characters. Despite the contrasts between these two stories, it is easy to agree that the worldbuilding in both of Corey’s literary works is what sets them apart.

The Kentucky mom charged with sexually abusing her 11-year-old son has a history of dating cops and heavy drinking ... at least according to her exes.

According to court documents obtained by The Post, Lauren Winans' baby daddies Daniel Newton and Derrick Carrico raised concerns that Lauren abuses alcohol and has "been with at least 16 different local deputies and police officers."

In a 2024 affidavit filed in his custody battle over their 9-year-old son, Newton wrote ... "Unfortunately, Lauren jumps from man to man."

Newton said "her children have been exposed to at least nine different men in Lauren's life" since her 2022 divorce from Carrico.

In his own filing for custody, Carrico claims Lauren brought their daughter over to now-husband Andy Winans' house for a sleepover in 2024 ... just one day after he'd signed an agreement with his ex-wife.

According to Carrico's affidavit, Lauren took her daughter to Andy's around 11 PM, and the little girl later told him ... "I want to tell you something, but I was told not to tell you, Nana, or Papa."

Carrico claimed ... "The child informed me that … she was made to sleep in the bed with her mom and the other man."

While that's disturbing enough on its own, Lauren and Andy got married about 3 weeks after his divorce from his ex was finalized.

Between this and her alleged alcohol abuse, the judge made both Newton and Carrico the primary residential caretakers of their kids.

The judge said her alleged drinking and mental health issues were "the biggest issue clearly before this court," but also stressed that it was also troubling how she decided to "hastily uproot her children from their maternal grandparents' residence and to require them to basically live with strangers (Andy and his three children)."

As you know, Lauren has recently been charged with first-degree sodomy, incest, and sexual abuse involving a child under age 12 ... for allegedly abusing her oldest son.

The charges come after the boy told his stepmom that his mom allegedly assaulted him on three separate occasions in 2022 ... when he was just 11 years old.

During Lauren's bond hearing Thursday, a detective testified that his investigation uncovered three alleged incidents of sexual abuse ... claiming she allegedly groped the boy twice and once engaged in "oral abuse."

The detective alleged that Lauren's son told her to stop during the third incident, but she told him the alleged abuse was "normal."

Lauren has pleaded not guilty to the charges and is being held on $250,000 bond in the county jail, where she's being closely monitored.
